EXCEPTIONS OF INTERVENOR JASON A. HOWTON TO THE PROPOSAL FOR DECISION
Intervenor Jason A. Howton, appearing pro se, respectfully and timely files these Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision issued in this docket on August 20, 2026 (Item No. 6441), and would respectfully show as follows:
TABLE OF EXCEPTIONS

Exceptions are numbered sequentially and appear in that order in the body, which follows the outline of the Proposal for Decision as Item No. 6442 requires. The "PFD §" column identifies the section of the Proposal for Decision to which each exception is addressed.
A note on the "omission" entries. Rule 22.262(a) governs the Commission's authority to change a finding the ALJs made. Where the ALJs made no finding, there is nothing to change. Those exceptions are addressed first to the ALJs under Rule 22.261(a), which permits them to "supplement or amend a proposal for decision in response to the exceptions," and alternatively to the Commission. They are the exceptions most likely to be granted and least likely to be reversed.
A note on where to begin. Mr. Howton's primary position is that the Application should be denied on either of the two independent grounds the Proposal for Decision identifies. If the Commission reaches the alternative route recommendation in Conclusion of Law 16, four of the exceptions below carry the argument and the remainder support them:
Exception 5 asks only that if the Commission changes Findings of Fact 22 through 29, it state in writing which ground under Rule 22.262(a) it is proceeding under, as Rule 22.262(b) requires. It asks for nothing if the Proposal for Decision is adopted.
Exception 19 identifies an arithmetic error. The Proposal for Decision states that Route 296 costs $20 million more than Route 894. That figure is the difference between Route 296 and Route 487. Against Route 894 the difference is $3,644,000, or 0.22%.
Exception 26 identifies Route 899, which shares thirty-seven of Route 894's forty-two links, carries the identical habitable-structure count of 85 and the identical species-habitat crossing of 461 feet, is shorter, costs 0.12% more, and avoids Links F20 and F23. No finding compares the two.
Exception 15 shows that the only route-specific reason given for setting Route 296 aside is proximity to three structures on one link, Link F34, and that the proximity can be mitigated within a tract Applicants already cross and whose owner already received notice of the Application.
I. INTRODUCTION
Mr. Howton is an intervenor of record in this proceeding. He owns and lives on 19.75 acres at 12808 FM 2843 in Bell County, where he has resided for twenty-two years, and he opposes Links F20 and F23 in every route in which they appear. His direct testimony and exhibits were admitted at Item No. 3925.
Mr. Howton supports the ALJs' recommendation that the Application be denied. He excepts to the Proposal for Decision in four respects.
A note on the form of many of these exceptions, and the standard they are offered under. A substantial number of the exceptions below ask the Commission to state as a finding of fact something the Proposal for Decision already establishes in its discussion. Mr. Howton is not asking the Commission to recite additional evidence, and he does not contend that a proposal for decision must catalogue everything in a record. The exceptions are narrower than that. In each instance the finding, as written, is narrower than the discussion it rests on, and the narrower finding is the one that carries forward into the order and supports a conclusion of law. A finding that states less than the record supporting it establishes is, to that extent, unsupported by a preponderance of the evidence within the meaning of Rule 22.262(a)(1)(B), and the conclusion drawn from it inherits the defect.
That is the form these exceptions take, and it is the form the administrative law judges in the companion docket accepted. There, intervenors identified findings that "fail to capture the full scope of the discussion in the body of the PFD," and the judges agreed that "certain FOF could be read to suggest a limitation when none was intended," amending two findings and adding four. Mr. Howton asks for the same relief on the same basis, and identifies for each exception the page of the Proposal for Decision on which the fuller discussion appears.
First, two of the ALJs' own findings do no work. Conclusion of Law 10 finds that Applicants violated Rule 22.52(a)(3) and attaches no consequence to it. The observation at page 149 that "the tariff exposure on steel and aluminum has not been analyzed" supports no finding of fact. Both should be completed.
Second, the ALJs identified an "asymmetry of input" arising from Applicants' post-meeting route expansion and placed it in Section VI, where they expressly declined to render findings because the questions presented were constitutional. That asymmetry is not solely constitutional. It bears directly on the reliability of the routing-criteria data compared in Section VIII, and it is governed by PURA § 37.056(c)(4) and 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B).
Third, and consequently, the alternative-route recommendation in Conclusion of Law 16 rests on comparative data that the record shows to be incomplete in one direction and unevenly gathered. Should the Commission decline to adopt the denial recommendation, Route 296, not Route 894, best serves the routing criteria.
Fourth, one principle governs both halves of this case, and Mr. Howton asks only that it be applied consistently to both.
The Administrative Law Judges withheld great weight from ERCOT's recommendation because it was not quantitatively substantiated. Finding of Fact 138 states that the recommendation is not "substantiated by quantifiable evidence of projected load growth." Finding of Fact 137 states that ERCOT "made no finding in the PBRP that it deemed the S&P Global load forecasts credible." Deference was withheld because the basis for it could not be tested.
Applicants' route ranking has the identical defect. The ALJs found that Applicants "did not assign weights to factors or sub-factors in their routing analysis and did not perform any sensitivity analysis to test Route 894's stability under alternative weighting schemes," and that Applicants' witness Perkins "agreed that different weighting choices could produce different route selections from the same candidate set of routes."
What that means in practice is on the record. On cross-examination, Applicants' witnesses agreed that Routes 894, 898, and 899 each carry 85 habitable structures within 500 feet; that Route 899 avoids Links F20 and F23 entirely; that Route 899 is shorter; and that the two routes' costs are "very close," a difference Ms. Cooley put at roughly $2 million. Asked whether, on habitable structures and cost, "the two factors that your routing analysis emphasized most," there was any material basis to prefer Route 894 over Route 899, Ms. Perkins answered: "If you're only focused on those factors that you've been discussing. But, as I've testified before, we looked at everything."
Mr. Howton does not suggest that answer was untrue. He observes that on this record it cannot be examined. Where no weights were assigned and no sensitivity analysis was performed, and where Applicants' own witness agrees that different weights would yield different routes, "we looked at everything" is not a quantified justification for preferring Route 894 over a route that ties it on both emphasized factors. It is an assurance, and the record supplies no means of testing it.
The consequence is the same whichever way the Commission resolves need, and each is independent of the other. If the Commission adopts the ALJs' recommendation, the Application is denied and Route 894 is never reached; Finding of Fact 140 carries that result even if great weight is afforded, because the ALJs found that the greater weight of the credible evidence is against the recommendation regardless. If the Commission instead finds that need is established, it must reach Conclusion of Law 16 and select a route, and it must do so on a record in which the preferred route's margin over an alternative that avoids Links F20 and F23 was never quantified, never weighted, and never tested. Neither path supports Route 894.
Mr. Howton does not ask the Commission to resolve any disputed count, and takes no position inconsistent with his own evidence.
The relief sought, in the alternative. Mr. Howton asks the Commission to adopt the ALJs' recommendation and deny the Application on either of the two independent grounds identified in the Proposal for Decision.
If the Commission concludes that denial is disproportionate to the notice violations found in Conclusions of Law 10, 11, and 15, then before approving the Application it must fashion a remedy that the Commission's rules do not supply and that PURA § 37.057 does not accommodate. PURA § 37.057 provides that the Commission "must approve or deny an application for a certificate for a new transmission facility not later than the 180th day after the date the application is filed," and supplies a mandamus remedy if it does not. The statute contains no good cause exception. Rule 22.52(a)(5) provides for "day-for-day extension of deadlines for intervention and for commission action on the application." Intervention closed April 27, 2026 and the hearing concluded June 12, 2026. A remedy that does not restore to the approximately 1,400 affected owners the opportunity Finding of Fact 26 says they lost is not a cure, and no such remedy can be completed within the statutory period absent Applicants' agreement.
If the Commission approves the Application without a cure, then the routing determination must account for the fact that the defect was not cured, and Route 296 rather than Route 894 should be selected.
II. JURISDICTION
No exception.
III. PROCEDURAL HISTORY
No exception.
IV. APPLICABLE LAW
No exception.
V. PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUES 1–4
A. Application Adequacy
No exception.
B. Notice
1. Notice of the Application
EXCEPTION 1: Conclusion of Law 10 states a violation and attaches no consequence to it.
Two different notice requirements are in play in this section, and they should not be run together.
• Rule 22.52(a)(3) governs notice of the Application, mailed on the date the application is filed to the owners of directly affected land. It is backward-looking: by the time it arrives, the routes are fixed and filed, and the recipient's remedy is to intervene and oppose.
• Rule 22.52(a)(4) governs the public meeting held before the application is filed. It is the only mechanism in the rule that operates while the routes can still change. It is not the hearing on the merits, and it is not a Commission proceeding at all; it is a meeting the utility holds in the affected community.
The ALJs found Applicants failed to comply with both. The two failures involve different landowners, different conduct, and different consequences. This exception addresses only subsection (a)(3). The public-meeting requirement is addressed at Exception 3.
The distinction matters immediately, because of what happened in the companion docket. In Docket No. 59315 the Chairman recommended rejecting the ALJs' Rule 22.52(a)(4) public-meeting holding. In the same memorandum he observed: "Regarding notice of the application, the ALJs did find that Oncor was compliant." This record is the opposite. Here the ALJs concluded that Applicants failed to comply with Rule 22.52(a)(3), notice of the Application itself, in addition to Rule 22.52(a)(4). The reasoning that disposed of the public-meeting question in Docket No. 59315 construes only the public-meeting rule. It says nothing about whether directly affected landowners received notice of the Application on the date it was filed, and it cannot, because in that docket they did. Applicants should not be permitted to carry a ruling about subsection (a)(4) across to subsection (a)(3).
Conclusion of Law 10 states that "Applicants did not comply with the notice requirements of Rule 22.52(a)(3)." The ALJs found that Applicants drew appraisal district data beginning December 8, 2025 and used it for notices mailed March 26, 2026, when the rule requires rolls current as of the filing date; that "[o]ver three dozen directly affected landowners did not receive notice of the Application timely"; and that Craig and Carleen Edwards of Link E12 "did not ever receive Application notice despite purchasing their home in August 2025." Those facts are reduced to Findings of Fact 41, 42, and 43.
The Edwards finding is missing. Findings of Fact 41 through 43 capture the late-noticed landowners and the rule failure. No finding captures the landowner who was never noticed at all. That is the most serious of the notice facts the ALJs found, and it exists only in the narrative at PFD 37.
No conclusion of law connects that violation to any remedy. It is the only violation the ALJs found that produces no consequence.
Under Rule 22.262(a)(1)(A), leaving a found violation without legal effect misapplies Rule 22.52. The rule's notice requirements exist to bring affected landowners into the proceeding before their rights are adjudicated. A landowner who was never noticed at all was denied that entirely, and the day-for-day extension in Rule 22.52(a)(5) cannot cure it now for the same reason the ALJs gave as to Rule 22.52(a)(4): the time in which the remedy could operate has passed.
Requested relief. A new conclusion of law stating that Applicants' violation of Rule 22.52(a)(3) independently supports denial of the Application; alternatively, a conclusion that the violation compounds the prejudice found in Findings of Fact 25, 26, and 29 and reinforces the conclusion in Conclusion of Law 15.
EXCEPTION 2: Applicants' own filing in this docket forecloses the remedy argument they will make.
This exception fortifies Conclusion of Law 15 in advance rather than seeking a change to it.
In Applicants' Response to John M. Burrow's Appeal of SOAH Order No. 25, Item No. 6056, at 5, Applicants argued:
"The day-for-day extension remedy in § 22.52(a)(5) applies to failures to comply with the notice requirements for filing an application as set forth in 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(1)-(3), specifically, the requirements to publish notice in newspapers, mail notice to municipalities and directly affected landowners, and provide proof of notice upon filing. The public participation meeting requirement of § 22.52(a)(4), by contrast, is a separate, pre-application obligation that is not always required. The rule mandates a public meeting only if 25 or more persons would be entitled to receive direct mail notice. Nothing in the text of the rule extends the day-for-day extension remedy to the public meeting context, and Mr. Burrow has cited no authority to the contrary."
The emphasized sentence matters as much as the rest. Applicants state that the public-meeting obligation is triggered by, and measured against, the class of persons "entitled to receive direct mail notice" of the application. That is the ALJs' reading of the trigger, in Applicants' own words, filed in this docket. It is also the reading the Chairman's memorandum in Docket No. 59315 does not engage: that memorandum answers how many meetings the rule requires, and says nothing about who must be noticed of the meeting it does require. On Applicants' own construction, the measuring class here is the roughly 4,200 owners entitled to Application notice, not the roughly 2,800 who existed when the meetings were held.
Applicants may not now argue that a day-for-day extension under Rule 22.52(a)(5) is the exclusive remedy for a Rule 22.52(a)(4) violation. If their reading in Item No. 6056 is correct, Rule 22.52(a)(5) never supplied a remedy for the violation the ALJs found, and the conclusion at PFD 46 that no lesser remedy remains is not merely correct but compelled by Applicants' own construction of the rule. If they now argue the contrary, they contradict the position they took in this docket to defeat Mr. Burrow's appeal.
Applicants have also foreclosed the extension itself. In a companion proceeding they argue that PURA § 37.057 is mandatory, that "the statute does not provide any commission right to extend," that there is "no 'good cause' exception, no tolling mechanism, and no provision authorizing the Commission or SOAH to suspend or continue the 180-day period," and that although 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(D) refers to extending beyond 180 days, the Commission "previously had statutory authority to go beyond 180 days that it no longer possesses." Rule 22.52(a)(5) provides for a day-for-day extension of deadlines "for intervention and for commission action on the application." On Applicants' own construction of the statute, the second half of that remedy is unavailable to the Commission as a matter of law. The first half closed with the intervention deadline. That is why the remedy the rule describes "is no longer available here."
Requested relief. A finding of fact reciting Applicants' position in Item No. 6056 as to the scope of Rule 22.52(a)(5), and a statement in the discussion supporting Conclusion of Law 15 that Applicants' own construction of the rule forecloses the argument that subsection (a)(5) supplies the exclusive remedy.
EXCEPTION 3: Rule 22.52(a)(4) required a further public meeting when roughly 1,400 additional landowners were brought within it, and the Commission's prior notice decisions do not reach these facts.
This exception was rebuilt on August 28, 2026. On August 27 Chairman Gleeson recommended that the Commission reject the Docket No. 59315 ALJs' Rule 22.52(a)(4) holding, delete Findings of Fact 28A, 29, 30, 30A, 30B, and 30C, and rewrite Conclusion of Law 11, reasoning that "[t]he plain language of the rule only requires that a utility hold at least one public meeting prior to filing its application" and that "Oncor's actions were consistent with Commission precedent." He cited three decisions, and those three are the ones this exception must answer:
• Application of the City of San Antonio to Amend Its CCN for the Scenic Loop 138-kV Transmission Line in Bexar County, Docket No. 51023, Order, Findings of Fact 21–31, Conclusion of Law 8 (Jan. 12, 2022);
• Application of LCRA Transmission Services Corporation to Amend Its CCN for the Cooks Point 138-kV Transmission Line in Burleson County, Docket No. 48358, Order, Findings of Fact 75, 85, Conclusion of Law 9 (June 17, 2019);
• Application of Oncor Electric Delivery Company to Amend a CCN for the Krum West to Anna 345-kV CREZ Transmission Line in Collin, Cooke, Denton, and Grayson Counties, Docket No. 38597, Order, Finding of Fact 34 (Mar. 7, 2011) (finding that 44 existing route links were modified, 22 new route links were added, and 1 route link was removed).
Before reaching those decisions, the rule's own text should be addressed, because it answers the question.
The first two sentences of Rule 22.52(a)(4) do different work:
"The utility must hold at least one public meeting prior to the filing of its licensing application if 25 or more persons would be entitled to receive direct mail notice of the application. Direct mail notice of the public meeting must be sent by first-class mail to each of the persons listed on the current county tax rolls as an owner of land within 300 feet of the centerline of a transmission project of 230 kV or less, an owner of land within 500 feet of the centerline of a transmission project greater than 230kV, [and] an owner of land adjacent to a property on which a substation ... will be located ...."
The first sentence states when a meeting is required and how many. The second states who must be told about it. Both are mandatory.
First, the condition is measured against the application, not against the meeting. The trigger is "if 25 or more persons would be entitled to receive direct mail notice of the application." The class that matters is therefore the class entitled to notice of the Application as filed: here, approximately 4,200 owners. The rule does not say "if 25 or more persons are entitled to notice as of whatever date the utility elects to hold a meeting." Read in its natural order, the sentence says: if 25 or more persons would be entitled to receive direct mail notice of the application, the utility must hold at least one public meeting prior to the filing of its licensing application. The condition defines the duty; the placement of the conditional clause at the end of the sentence does not change what it modifies.
Second, "at least one" is a floor, not a safe harbor. The phrase fixes a minimum. It does not cap the requirement, and it does not convert a meeting that preceded the creation of 400 miles of route links into compliance as to the landowners on those links. On the reading applied in Docket No. 59315, "at least one" functions as "never more than one," which is the opposite of what the words say and would render "at least" surplusage. A utility could then hold a single meeting on a preliminary corridor and afterward relocate the project entirely. The Commission need not decide that outer case. It need only decide whether one meeting, held before roughly 400 miles of links existed, discharged the duty as to the approximately 1,400 owners those links brought within the rule.
The rule supplies its own stopping point, and Applicants' contrary reading has no stopping point at all. Applicants answer, in a companion proceeding, that this construction "ignore[s] the necessary chronological order of the process by arguing that 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(4) requires that Oncor know its final routing alternatives before receiving feedback from the public on routing." It does not. Mr. Howton does not contend that every link modification re-triggers a meeting, or that the meeting must display the final routes. The trigger the rule states is numerical, and it supplies the limit: a further meeting is owed when the persons newly entitled to notice of the application themselves satisfy the rule's threshold. Here roughly 1,400 owners were newly brought within it, more than fifty times the rule's own figure of 25.
The administrative law judges in the companion docket stated the same limit, on the same rule, in the same posture:
"For example, a utility performing a routing study may count fewer than 25 owners of directly affected land based on preliminary links and may decide no public meeting is required pursuant to Rule 22.52(a)(4). If by the filing of the application, it is determined that there are 25 or more owners of directly affected land, the utility is subject to the public meeting requirement and must notice and convene that meeting prior to filing its application. It matters not that at some earlier point during the routing study there were fewer than 25 owners of directly affected land."
Those judges also noted that the phrase "at least" in the first sentence "forms a floor," and that if it meant a second meeting could never be required, "the 'at least' would be superfluous."
Applicants' reading is the one with no limiting principle. As the companion ALJs put it, defining the "transmission project" by reference to the links as they stood on the day of the meeting "presents a question of when changes to a 'transmission project' become so significant that the project in the application is no longer the same project that was addressed at the public meeting. If, following a public meeting, a utility deleted all preliminary links and generated entirely new link segments, would the utility be entitled to rely on the previously held public meeting under Oncor's construction? Or would this constitute a new project requiring a new public meeting?" On Applicants' construction a utility could discard every link it displayed and still rely on the meeting it held. The rule's numerical trigger avoids that result; Applicants' reading invites it.
Third, and independent of how many meetings the first sentence requires, the second sentence was not satisfied. The duty to send direct mail notice of the public meeting to "each of the persons" within 500 feet of the centerline carries no "at least one" qualifier and no exception. The ALJs found it was not done: "No landowner within the expanded study area or within 500 feet of the centerline of the newly created links received notice of a public meeting." That finding describes a failure of the second sentence on its own terms. It stands whether the first sentence required one meeting or two.
The anticipated answer, and why it does not work. Applicants will say those owners were not within 500 feet of any centerline when the meeting was held, so no notice was owed then. That is true, and it is the difficulty rather than the answer. The rule ties the meeting to the application: the meeting must occur "prior to the filing of its licensing application," and the persons entitled to notice of it are defined by the centerline of the project for which the application is made. A utility that finalizes its routes after its only meeting has not thereby complied; it has made compliance impossible through its own sequencing. Nothing prevented a further meeting, and Applicants' own conduct shows it. They did not hold one meeting; they held three: June 16, 2025 at the Salado ISD Meadows Room, June 17, 2025 at the Lampasas ISD Old Middle School Cafeteria, and June 18, 2025 at the Menard County Community Center. Applicants therefore understood that "at least one" sets a floor and that additional meetings were both permitted and practicable; they held two more than the minimum when the affected class was the one they had identified. They then filed the Application on March 26, 2026, more than nine months after the last meeting, without holding another for the roughly 1,400 owners added in the interim.
Fourth, the purpose of the two subsections confirms the distinction. Notice of the application under Rule 22.52(a)(3) tells a landowner that routes have been chosen and that he may intervene to oppose them. The public meeting under Rule 22.52(a)(4) is the only step in the rule at which a landowner can identify a constraint before the routes are fixed. Treating the former as a substitute for the latter reads the public-meeting requirement out of the rule, and it is precisely the substitution the ALJs found caused prejudice: for the links added after the meetings, "no property owner (some 1,400) was able to identify routing constraints or address concerns at a public meeting, to their prejudice."
Mr. Howton does not contend that the June 2025 meetings were deficient as to the landowners then on the proposed routes. No party has challenged that, and he does not. His contention is narrower: the approximately 1,400 owners brought within the rule by links added afterward were never given the meeting the rule requires, and the second sentence's mailing duty was never performed as to any of them.
If the Commission nevertheless adheres to the construction it applied on August 28, 2026, the three decisions relied upon still do not reach these facts. Mr. Howton does not dispute any of those holdings, and does not ask the Commission to overrule them. Each is distinguishable on its face, and the distinctions are structural rather than factual.
Docket Nos. 51023 and 48358 were 138-kV lines in a single county. Mr. Howton does not suggest the public-meeting requirement was inapplicable in those cases; it applied. The distinction is in the scope of the class and, more importantly, in what the orders decided. Rule 22.52(a)(4) sets the direct-mail radius for public-meeting notice at 300 feet from the centerline "of a transmission project of 230 kV or less," and at 500 feet "of a transmission project greater than 230 kV." A 138-kV project draws the narrower 300-foot radius; this Project, at 765 kV, draws the 500-foot radius. Each case involved one county: Bexar in Docket No. 51023, Burleson in Docket No. 48358.
The dispositive distinction is not scale, it is subject matter. Neither order decided what happens when the class of persons entitled to notice of the application expands materially after the public meetings are held and no further meeting is offered. That question, the one Findings of Fact 22 through 29 present, was not before the Commission in either case.
Docket No. 37951 is subject to the same distinction. Applicants also rely on Application of Oncor Electric Delivery Company to Amend a Certificate of Convenience and Necessity for the Clear Crossing to Dermott 345-kV CREZ Transmission Line, Docket No. 37951, Final Order, Findings of Fact 63–69 (Oct. 5, 2010), described in their own briefing as "explaining that the applicant modified, added, and deleted links after the three public meetings that were held based on further analysis and public input." Like Docket No. 38597, it is a CREZ proceeding, and the discussion below applies to it in full.
Docket No. 38597 was a CREZ line, decided under a statute that relieved the Commission of the findings at issue here. PURA § 39.904(h) provided that "[i]n considering an application for a certificate of public convenience and necessity for a transmission project intended to serve a competitive renewable energy zone, the commission is not required to consider the factors provided by Sections 37.056(c)(1) and (2)." The ALJs made the same point about CREZ generally at PFD 57: no CREZ transmission service provider had to "prove that the construction" "is necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public." A decision about the adequacy of public-meeting notice in a proceeding where the Legislature had already made the need determination, and where the Commission was excused from two of the § 37.056(c) factors, does not measure the adequacy of public-meeting notice in a proceeding where Applicants bear the full burden under § 37.056(a) and where the ALJs found that burden unmet.
The scale comparison also runs the wrong way for Applicants. Finding of Fact 34 in Docket No. 38597 records 44 links modified, 22 added, and 1 removed. Here the ALJs found a post-meeting expansion of hundreds of miles of new route links and roughly 1,400 newly affected landowners, raising the noticed class from approximately 2,800 to more than 4,200. Docket No. 38597 is the Chairman's closest case on the mechanics and his furthest case on the magnitude.
The Commission's stated rationale does not reach these findings either. In Docket No. 59315 the Commission reasoned that "[u]nlike 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(1)–(a)(3), which provide specific instructions as to who and when notice of the application must be sent, subsection (a)(4) does not specify when the utility is to hold a public meeting other than requiring the utility to hold a public meeting prior to filing the application," and that landowners on later-added links "received notice of the application[] and therefore had an opportunity to intervene and participate." That reasoning addresses the first sentence of the rule: how many meetings, and when. It does not address the second sentence, which requires that direct mail notice of the meeting be sent to each person within 500 feet of the centerline and which Finding of Fact 24 finds was not done here. And even taken at its full breadth, it does not answer what the ALJs found here at Finding of Fact 26: that some 1,400 owners were unable "to identify routing constraints or address concerns at a public meeting, to their prejudice." An opportunity to intervene after the routes are fixed and filed is not the same opportunity as the one the meeting provides, which is the opportunity to shape the routes before they are fixed. That is the asymmetry Exceptions 6 and 13 develop, and it is a routing question under PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(A) whatever the answer on notice compliance.
The distinction that matters is not scale, and Mr. Howton does not rest on scale. Docket No. 59315 involved a comparable and in fact larger group: the administrative law judges there found that 1,645 landowners owned property within 520 feet of a link added or modified after the June 2025 public meetings. The number of affected owners therefore cannot be what separates the two dockets, and Mr. Howton does not argue that it is.
What separates them is the posture of the recommendation. In Docket No. 59315 the administrative law judges found the violation but expressly "decline[d] to recommend a specific sanction for the notice failure, leaving it to the Commission's discretion." The Commission was therefore free to correct the legal holding without disturbing any recommended disposition. Here the administrative law judges did not leave the consequence open. They recommended denial, and Conclusion of Law 15 rests the recommendation in part on the notice failure. Reversing the holding in this docket is not a clarification of law with no operative effect; it removes a stated ground for the ALJs' disposition, and Rule 22.262(b) requires the Commission to say so in writing and to identify the ground on which it proceeds.
One further feature of this rule is worth the Commission's attention. The administrative law judges in the companion docket observed that "it does not appear that a court has construed Rule 22.52(a)(4)." Mr. Howton has found none either. The construction the Commission adopted on August 28, 2026 is therefore its own, unreviewed, and of first impression, which is a reason for the written statement of reasons Rule 22.262(b) requires rather than a reason to withhold it.
The deadline argues for deciding, not for approving. PURA § 37.057 requires the Commission to "approve or deny" the application within 180 days, and states one consequence for missing it: "a party may seek a writ of mandamus in a district court of Travis County to compel the commission to decide on the application." Missing the deadline does not approve the Application, does not deprive the Commission of jurisdiction, and does not convert a record that will not support the required findings into one that will. Mr. Howton raises this because the schedule compression the ALJs describe, and their conclusion that "the remedy identified by the rule is no longer available here," PFD at 46, will be urged as a reason the Commission must act. It is a reason to decide. Denial is a decision, and it satisfies the statute exactly as approval would.
None of the three involved a 180-day statutory deadline. PURA § 37.057 was amended by HB 5066 to impose the 180-day period that governs this proceeding, and the ALJs concluded that on this schedule "the remedy identified by the rule is no longer available here." The compression that deadline produces is why. In a proceeding with a one-year clock under 16 TAC § 25.101(b) and "good cause" available to extend it, a notice defect discovered mid-case can be cured by holding a meeting and extending the schedule. Here it cannot, because Applicants did not waive mandamus under PURA § 37.057 and the day-for-day extension in Rule 22.52(a)(5) has nothing left to extend. That is not a difference in degree. It is the difference between a rule violation with a remedy and a rule violation without one.
Applicants' additional authorities. Applicants rely in a companion proceeding on Docket No. 45624 and Docket No. 49523 as well, for the proposition that public meeting notice is measured by the preliminary routes displayed at the meeting, even where routes are later modified, and that only one meeting is required. Mr. Howton does not dispute those holdings either. They do not answer this record, for three further reasons.
First, the rule's threshold. The ALJs read Rule 22.52(a)(4) as written: the requirement of "at least one" public meeting is a minimum "tied to 'if 25 or more persons would be entitled to receive direct mail notice of the application.'" PFD at 44. Where the class entitled to application notice grows past that threshold after the meeting, the minimum has not been met as to the persons newly within it. None of the cited dockets addressed that question, and none involved a post-meeting expansion of approximately 400 miles of route links and approximately 1,400 landowners, raising the affected class from roughly 2,800 to roughly 4,200. The ALJs said so: the reading Applicants urge "is incorrect, especially here," and "when a project of this scale and complexity adds ... hundreds of miles of new route links and roughly 1,400 new landowners entitled to application notice, a utility cannot force newly affected landowners entitled to application notice out of the community input process if there are 25 or more."
Second, the record distinguishes them on the facts. In Docket No. 45624 and Docket No. 49523 the post-meeting changes were made in response to community feedback. Here the Environmental Assessment records something different: "Following the public open house meetings, Oncor and LCRA TSC asked Kimley-Horn and Halff to evaluate and consider expansion of the breadth of alternative route links throughout the study area." The expansion was requested by Applicants after the meetings. It was not a refinement of the routes the public commented on.
Third, on SOAH Order No. 25. Applicants note that intervenors raised a similar argument in this docket, that SOAH Order No. 25 denied the motion, and that the Commission "voted to not add John M. Burrow's Appeal of SOAH Order No. 25 to any open meeting agenda." Neither disposition reaches the question now presented. SOAH Order No. 25 denied a motion for a 206-day continuance filed before the hearing. It resolved whether the proceeding should be delayed, not whether Applicants complied with Rule 22.52(a)(4) or what remedy remains after the record closed. And under Rule 22.123(a)(7)(A), an interim appeal that no commissioner places on an agenda within 20 days "is deemed denied." A deemed denial is not an adjudication, and Rule 22.123(a)(1) provides that interim orders "are not subject to exceptions or motions for rehearing," which is why the question arrives here for the first time.
Requested relief. Findings of fact that:
AG. This Project is a transmission project greater than 230 kV crossing fifteen counties, for which more than 4,200 landowners were entitled to notice of the Application, and is subject to the 180-day deadline in PURA § 37.057, which contains no good cause exception.
EXCEPTION 4: Rule 22.52(a)(5) states a consequence for the violation found, and the violation goes to the sufficiency of the evidence in any event.
Applicants argue in a companion proceeding that under AC Interests, L.P. v. Texas Commission on Environmental Quality, 543 S.W.3d 703, 714 (Tex. 2018), a procedural provision that specifies no consequence for noncompliance is presumed directory rather than mandatory, and that Rule 22.52(a)(4) therefore cannot require denial. They pair it with Texas Government Code § 2001.174(2)(F) to argue that denial on notice grounds would be an abuse of discretion.
The premise fails on the text. Rule 22.52(a)(5) provides: "Failure to provide notice in accordance with this section will be cause for day-for-day extension of deadlines for intervention and for commission action on the application." Rule 22.52(a)(4) is within this section. Because the rule already expresses a consequence, the premise of AC Interests is absent here and it is not the applicable framework.
The exception does not depend on resolving that. The violation the ALJs found is not only a procedural defect. It is a statement about the record. Findings of Fact 25, 26, and 29 establish that approximately 1,400 owners, about one third of the affected class, had no meeting at which to identify routing constraints before the routes were fixed, and that this occurred to their prejudice. PURA § 37.056 requires the Commission to find affirmatively that the certificate is necessary and to consider community values and the other statutory factors. The Commission is not being asked to invent a consequence. It is being asked to decline to make findings the record does not support.
Requested relief. A conclusion of law that Rule 22.52(a)(5) states a consequence for failure to provide notice in accordance with Rule 22.52, including subsection (a)(4); and that the prejudice found in Findings of Fact 25, 26, and 29 bears on the sufficiency of the evidence supporting the findings PURA § 37.056(c)(4) requires.
2. Notice of Public Meeting
Findings of Fact 22 through 30 are sound as written and should be adopted. Proposed additions appear at Exception 14.
EXCEPTION 5: If the Commission adopts the construction of Rule 22.52(a)(4) it applied on August 28, 2026, Rule 22.262(b) requires it to state the specific reason and legal basis for altering Findings of Fact 22 through 29, which remain true and remain relevant to community values however the rule is construed.
This exception is pleaded in the alternative and is Mr. Howton's most important request in this section. It asks for nothing if the Commission adopts the Proposal for Decision as written. It matters only if the Commission does not, and Item No. 6442 permits no later opportunity to raise it.
What happened in the companion docket. On August 27, 2026, Chairman Gleeson recommended that the Commission reject the Docket No. 59315 ALJs' holding that Oncor failed to comply with Rule 22.52(a)(4), on a legal ground: "Ultimately, I believe the ALJs misinterpreted the requirements in our rule."
The Commission adopted that recommendation the following day. Docket No. 59315, Order (Aug. 28, 2026) (Item No. 5819). The Order holds that Rule 22.52(a)(4) "does not expressly or implicitly require that Oncor hold an additional public meeting in the event [it] expands the study area," reasoning that "[u]nlike 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(1)–(a)(3), which provide specific instructions as to who and when notice of the application must be sent, subsection (a)(4) does not specify when the utility is to hold a public meeting other than requiring the utility to hold a public meeting prior to filing the application." It further reasons that although "landowners on links added after the public meeting may not have received notice of the public meeting," they received notice of the application "and therefore[] had an opportunity to intervene and participate." The Order then states: "Accordingly, findings of fact 28A, 29, 30, 30A, 30B, and 30C should be deleted and conclusion of law 11 should be modified because the ALJ did not properly interpret Commission rule and Commission policy."
Mr. Howton takes the Commission at its word that this is the construction it has adopted, and frames this exception accordingly. He does not contend the Commission lacked authority to act as it did.
The rule states two separate grounds. 16 TAC § 22.262(a) provides that the Commission may change a finding of fact or conclusion of law made by the administrative law judge only if the Commission:
"(1) determines that the administrative law judge:
(A) did not properly apply or interpret applicable law, commission rules or policies, or prior administrative decisions; or
(B) issued a finding of fact that is not supported by a preponderance of the evidence; or
(2) determines that a commission policy or a prior administrative decision on which the administrative law judge relied is incorrect or should be changed."
And subsection (b): "The commission will state in writing the specific reason and legal basis for its determination under subsection (a)."
Grounds (A) and (B) are distinct, and they do different work. Ground (A) addresses an error of law: a misapplication or misinterpretation of law, rule, policy, or prior decision. Ground (B) addresses an error of proof: a finding unsupported by a preponderance of the evidence. Either may support changing a finding of fact or a conclusion of law; the rule's opening words say so. But the two grounds do not reach the same defect, and subsection (b) requires the Commission to say which one it is invoking and why: "The commission will state in writing the specific reason and legal basis for its determination under subsection (a)."
Mr. Howton's point is narrow and is directed at subsection (b), not at the Commission's authority. A determination that the ALJs misread Rule 22.52(a)(4) is a determination under ground (A). It establishes that the ALJs drew the wrong legal consequence from the facts they found. It does not, without more, establish that any of those facts is untrue. Where the Commission changes or deletes a historical finding on a ground (A) rationale, subsection (b) requires it to state the specific reason and legal basis for concluding that its interpretation of the rule requires altering that factual finding, not merely the conclusion drawn from it.
Applied to this record. The findings in this docket that correspond to those deleted in Docket No. 59315 are Findings of Fact 22 through 30. Read them as they are written:
22. After the June 2025 public meetings and based on information gathered through the public meetings, Applicants expanded the study area to include options further north in Lampasas, San Saba, and McCulloch Counties and added approximately 400 miles of new route links, which brought approximately 1,400 additional landowners within the class entitled to direct mail notice of the Application, raising the affected landowners from roughly 2,800 to roughly 4,200.
23. No other public meetings were held prior to the filing of the Application.
24. No landowner within the expanded study area or within 500 feet of the centerline of the newly created links received notice of a public meeting.
25. Approximately 1,400 landowners with property within 520 feet of the links added or modified after the June 2025 public meetings who were entitled to receive direct mail notice of the Application did not receive notice of a public meeting.
26. For the links that Applicants added or modified following the June 2025 public meetings, no property owner (some 1,400) was able to identify routing constraints or address concerns at a public meeting, to their prejudice.
27. Approximately 4,200 written notices of the Application were mailed to property owners.
28. The Project as filed in the Application differed significantly and materially from the project that was presented at the June 2025 public meetings.
29. Applicants only provided opportunities for community value input to about two-thirds of affected property owners entitled to notice of the Application.
30. The Application should be denied because Applicants deprived approximately 1,400 landowners, to their prejudice, of the process due them under 16 Texas Administrative Code § (Rule) 22.52(a)(4) for public meeting.
Findings of Fact 22 through 29 are historical facts. How many miles of link were added; how many meetings were held; who received notice of them; how many notices of the Application were mailed; whether the filed project differed from the one presented. Every one of those propositions is true or false without reference to how Rule 22.52(a)(4) is construed. The numbers come from Applicants' own affidavits and exhibits and are not disputed. A different reading of the rule changes what those facts mean; it does not make them untrue.
Finding of Fact 30 is different, and Mr. Howton says so plainly. It is a legal conclusion in the form of a finding: it states the legal consequence ("should be denied because ... the process due them under ... Rule 22.52(a)(4)"). Together with Conclusion of Law 11, it is what a ground (A) determination most directly reaches. Mr. Howton opposes changing it, for the reasons given in Exceptions 3 and 4. But he acknowledges that if the Commission adopts the construction it applied in Docket No. 59315, Finding of Fact 30 and Conclusion of Law 11 are the provisions squarely before it under Rule 22.262(a)(1)(A).
The historical findings are not in the same position. Findings of Fact 22 through 29 would remain accurate under either reading of Rule 22.52(a)(4), and Mr. Howton asks only that if the Commission alters them, it comply with subsection (b) by stating why its interpretation of the rule requires altering a factual finding rather than the conclusion drawn from it.
Two findings must survive whatever the Commission concludes about notice, because they support a different statutory determination.
Finding of Fact 29 states that Applicants "only provided opportunities for community value input to about two-thirds of affected property owners entitled to notice of the Application." That is not a finding about notice compliance. It is a finding about community values, which PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(A) requires the Commission to consider and which 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B) reaches through its direction that a line be "routed to the extent reasonable to moderate the impact on the affected community and landowners." Whether Rule 22.52(a)(4) was violated and whether the record contains adequate community-values evidence are separate questions with separate legal sources. The Commission may answer the first in Applicants' favor and still be unable to answer the second without Finding of Fact 29 before it.
Finding of Fact 28 states that the Project as filed "differed significantly and materially from the project that was presented at the June 2025 public meetings." That finding bears on the weight of every questionnaire and comment gathered at those meetings, which Findings of Fact 169 through 173 treat as the evidentiary basis for the community-values analysis. If the meetings addressed a materially different project, the input they produced is worth less as evidence about the project actually before the Commission. That is a sufficiency question under PURA § 37.056(c)(4), and it does not depend on any rule violation.
Requested relief. In the alternative, and only if the Commission declines to adopt Conclusion of Law 11 and Finding of Fact 30 as written:
AL. That the Commission preserve Findings of Fact 22 through 29 and state in writing, as Rule 22.262(b) requires, the specific reason and legal basis for any finding it does change, identifying whether it proceeds under Rule 22.262(a)(1)(A), Rule 22.262(a)(1)(B), or Rule 22.262(a)(2) as to each.
AM. That Findings of Fact 28 and 29 be carried into Section VIII as findings bearing on community values under PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(A), on the requirement of 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B) that the line be routed to the extent reasonable to moderate the impact on the affected community and landowners, and on the completeness of the comparative routing data, as requested in Exceptions 6 and 14.

"Second, the notice. For hundreds of landowners who were not invited to public meetings, nine months before the Application notice on March 26, 2026, they had limited time to act."
"Third, the asymmetry of public input. EXCEPTION 9: The statute assigns the determination of load to the transmission service provider.
At PFD 55 the ALJs quote two provisions. They do different work, and Mr. Howton separates them because the distinction is what makes this exception useful.
PURA § 39.166(a)(1) governs the reliability plan. It directs the Commission to have ERCOT "identify each region in which transmission capacity is insufficient to meet the region's existing and forecasted electrical load, as reasonably determined by the certificated transmission service provider." The load figure on which ERCOT identifies a region is therefore not ERCOT's determination. It is the transmission service provider's, and ERCOT takes it as given.
PURA § 37.056(c-1) governs this proceeding. It provides that in considering the need for additional service under Subsection (c)(2) for a reliability transmission project serving the ERCOT power region, or under Subsection (c)(4)(F), "the commission must consider the historical load, forecasted load growth, and additional load currently seeking interconnection, including load for which the electric utility has yet to sign an interconnection agreement, as determined by the electric utility with the responsibility for serving the load." The ALJs add: "The 'electric utility' includes providers like Applicants, Oncor and LCRA."
ERCOT states the consequence in the Application itself: the study relies on "data provided by TDSPs—and relied upon by ERCOT for the purposes of this study, as required by statute," with footnote 7 citing PURA § 39.166(a)(1).
The first provision explains the ALJs' finding at PFD 91–92 that "ERCOT made no finding in the PBRP that it deemed the S&P Global load forecasts credible." ERCOT made no such finding because § 39.166(a)(1) did not assign that determination to ERCOT. It assigned it to the certificated transmission service provider: here, Applicants. That is a structural feature of the statute, not a failing of any individual, and it goes directly to the weight owed ERCOT's recommendation under Rule 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii)(II). It fortifies Conclusion of Law 13.
The second provision explains why the weight owed that recommendation cannot end the inquiry. Section 37.056(c-1) puts the utility's own load determination before the Commission as the thing the Commission "must consider." The statute does not direct the Commission to consider ERCOT's endorsement of that determination; it directs the Commission to consider the determination itself. A recommendation that rests on an input the recommending organization never evaluated cannot discharge the Commission's obligation to consider that input. The two provisions run in the same direction: the load figure was the utility's throughout, and it is the utility's figure the Commission is required to examine.
Requested relief. Findings of fact that:
T. Under PURA § 39.166(a)(1), the existing and forecasted electrical load by reference to which the independent organization identifies a region of insufficient transmission capacity is that reasonably determined by the certificated transmission service provider; and ERCOT relied on load data provided by the transmission and distribution service providers as required by statute.
AS. Under PURA § 37.056(c-1), the historical load, forecasted load growth, and additional load currently seeking interconnection that the Commission must consider in determining the need for additional service are those determined by the electric utility with the responsibility for serving the load.
Supporting context, if wanted: ERCOT's February 2024 Regional Planning Group status presentation records that of the 23,958 MW modeled for 2030, 11,995 MW was "Additional Load," footnoted as "Mainly datacenter/crypto load," with ERCOT's own observation that "the total amount of additional non-oil & gas load is almost the same as the oil & gas load."
EXCEPTION 10: Great weight is conditional. The condition failed here, and the reason the Commission wrote the condition is the reason it matters.
This exception seeks no change to the Proposal for Decision. It fortifies Findings of Fact 133 through 140 and Conclusion of Law 13 against the argument Applicants will make in reply, and against a conclusion of law the Commission adopted in a companion docket on August 28, 2026.
The conclusion this exception defends. The ALJs found that ERCOT's PBRP 765-kV import paths recommendation "should not be given great weight under Rule 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii)(II)(-a-)," FoF 139, and, independently, that "[e]ven affording great weight to ERCOT's PBRP 765-kV recommendation, the greater weight of the credible evidence is against the recommendation," FoF 140. Conclusion of Law 13 states that ERCOT's PBRP recommendation is not entitled to great weight in the determination of need for this reliability project. Those are two separate holdings, and the second does not depend on the first.
The competing conclusion. On August 27, 2026, Chairman Gleeson recommended that the Commission add to the orders in Docket Nos. 59029 and 59315 a conclusion of law that "[a] recommendation from ERCOT is entitled to great weight in the determination of need for a reliability project in accordance with 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii)(II)." Applicants will present that conclusion here as controlling. It is not, for three reasons.
First, the rule states a condition, and the conclusion states only the command. Rule 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii)(II) provides that when evaluating reliability for a proposed project in the ERCOT region, "the commission will consider and any review conducted by ERCOT must incorporate the historical load, forecasted load growth, and additional load currently seeking interconnection. The forecasted load growth and additional load currently seeking interconnection must be substantiated by quantifiable evidence of projected load growth." Only then does the subclause provide that "[t]he commission will give great weight to" the recommendation of a PURA § 39.151 organization. The condition precedes the command in the text and governs it. The ALJs read the rule that way.
A conclusion of law reciting the command in the abstract is not inconsistent with Findings of Fact 137 through 139. Both can stand. A recommendation is entitled to great weight when the rule's condition is satisfied; on this record the condition was not satisfied, because "ERCOT made no finding in the PBRP that it deemed the S&P Global load forecasts credible." FoF 137. The Commission need not choose between the two propositions. It need only apply the second to this record.
Second, the Commission wrote the condition for exactly this situation, and said so. The substantiation requirement was added to Rule 25.101 in Project No. 53403. In the order adopting it, the Commission explained why:
"If ERCOT is not able to evaluate, and when necessary, reject, evidence of load growth it may result in an overestimation of load growth and an overbuild of transmission. Given the significant number of megawatts that are currently seeking interconnection but are not yet contractually committed, the risk of such a overbuild is not hypothetical. Accordingly, the commission modifies the rule to require that load growth forecasts are substantiated by quantifiable evidence."
That passage is the answer to the argument that the substantiation clause is a technicality. The clause exists so that ERCOT can screen out load that will not materialize, and the Commission adopted it because the risk of building transmission for load that never arrives "is not hypothetical." Here the screen was never applied. ERCOT did not evaluate the S&P Global forecast, did not deem it credible, and used it because HB 5066 directed it to use load provided by the certificated transmission service provider. FoF 136, 137. Withholding great weight in that circumstance is not a penalty. It is the rule operating as designed.
The record supplies the concrete case. In Project No. 55999 the Commission granted ERCOT a good cause exception to adjust downward the same category of substantiated load for the 2025 Regional Transmission Plan, finding that "[g]ood cause exists due to the recent actual experience . . . of previously forecasted loads coming into service at lower megawatt levels than initially claimed." FoF 133, 134. The Commission has already found, in another proceeding, that this category of load overstated itself.
Third, great weight has never meant conclusive weight, and the Austin Court of Appeals has said so about an ERCOT report in a CCN appeal the Commission won.
In Hammack v. Public Utility Commission of Texas, landowners challenged a CCN the Commission granted to Central Power and Light, arguing among other things that the finding of need was unsupported. The court affirmed. In doing so it described the role of the ERCOT report in the need determination:
"The determination of public need is made at the time of the hearing. The ERCOT report is but one part of the evidence the commission relied on in making this determination. Additionally, the Commission is not constrained by the public need identified in the application for a CCN. The facets of public need may very well be fluid. Addressing one need may create another, as is evidenced in this case."
The report at issue there described itself in terms the Commission should find familiar:
"Due to its very nature, transmission planning is a continuous process. Therefore, conclusions reached in this report are a snapshot in time that can change with the addition (or elimination) of plans for new generation, transmission facilities, equipment, or loads."
Three propositions follow, and none of them requires the Commission to disturb anything it did on August 28:
1. Need is determined on the hearing record, as of the hearing. That is what the ALJs did. It is also the answer to the argument that finding no need here collaterally attacks the order approving the PBRP. The Commission reserved this question for this proceeding in writing. See Exception 7, proposed Finding D.
2. The ERCOT recommendation is one part of the evidence, not a substitute for it. Hammack said so in a case where the Commission's need finding was upheld, which means the proposition cannot be dismissed as a landowner's gloss. Applicants cannot distinguish Hammack as a case that went the other way. It did not.
3. A transmission plan is a snapshot that changes as generation, facilities, and loads change. The record shows those changes. Applicants admitted in discovery that no ERCOT or Oncor study parses out central Texas's net generation position under any scenario, that no determination was made whether central Texas can serve local load and simultaneously export west at design capacity, and that no sensitivity analysis was performed. Howton Ex. JAH-32, Nos. 1-96, 1-97, 1-100; PFD at 70, 86–87. See Exception 11.
The arithmetic Applicants invite. Applicants ask the Commission to treat "great weight" as though weight alone decides the question. It does not. Weight is applied to evidence; it does not manufacture it. Where the underlying forecast was never screened by the organization whose expertise the rule credits, multiplying it changes nothing. Great weight applied to an unsubstantiated foundation yields an unsubstantiated result with more decimal places.
Requested relief. Findings of fact and a conclusion of law that:
AD. The substantiation requirement in 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii)(II) was adopted in Project No. 53403 to permit ERCOT to evaluate and, when necessary, reject evidence of load growth, because the risk of an overbuild of transmission arising from load that is seeking interconnection but not contractually committed is not hypothetical.
AE. ERCOT did not apply that evaluation to the S&P Global load forecast underlying the Permian Basin Reliability Plan Study.
CL-7. A recommendation of an organization meeting the requirements of PURA § 39.151 is entitled to great weight under 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii)(II) when the forecasted load growth and additional load currently seeking interconnection on which it rests are substantiated by quantifiable evidence of projected load growth. Great weight is not conclusive weight, and it does not relieve the Commission of its independent obligation under PURA § 37.056(a) to determine on the record whether the certificate is necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public.

A note on the burden. Applicants argue in a companion proceeding that "no party ... has introduced any evidence to rebut the conclusions of these studies" and that "[t]here is no evidence in the record on which the Commission could reasonably determine there is no electrical need for this project." The ALJs did not find that the Project is unnecessary. They found that Applicants failed to show it is necessary, and the findings rest on Applicants' own responses to discovery in this docket. B. Intervenor Concerns Regarding Routing Methodology
EXCEPTION 12: Finding of Fact 160 rests on an unstated and untested weighting.
The ALJs record that "Applicants did not assign weights to factors or sub-factors in their routing analysis and did not perform any sensitivity analysis to test Route 894's stability under alternative weighting schemes," and that "Applicants witness Perkins agreed that different weighting choices could produce different route selections from the same candidate set of routes."
Mr. Howton does not ask the Commission to adopt a mathematical routing methodology. He agrees with the principle the ALJs credited from Smitherman, McAdams, and Poole that route selection is a balancing of factors rather than an arithmetic exercise, and asks that it be applied consistently, including to Applicants' own selection.
The narrower point is this. No Focus Route differs from Route 894 by more than 2.04% in estimated cost or 2.62% in length, and the four routes span 3.03% on cost and 7.52 miles (3.40%) on length. Applicants' own witness conceded that different weightings produce different selections from the same candidate set. No sensitivity analysis was performed. On that record, a finding that Route 894 "presents an appropriate balance of routing factors" is not supported by a preponderance of the evidence within the meaning of Rule 22.262(a)(1)(B), because the balance asserted was never tested.
The Proposal for Decision contains a worked example of the unstated weighting, and it runs against Route 894. Applicants identified Route 894 Western Mod 1 as a route of interest. It is Route 894 with a different western portion: it "utilizes Links N12-P1 rather than Route 894's N3-P2-R1," leaving the Bell County links untouched. On Applicants' own comparative table it carries 80 habitable structures within 500 feet, five fewer than Route 894's 85. The ALJs did not select it, and the reason they gave was paralleling: Route 894 Western Mod 1 "has less length parallel to existing compatible ROW than the Focus Routes."
Mr. Howton does not contend that Route 894 Western Mod 1 should have been selected, and he does not advocate it. He offers it because it shows what Finding of Fact 160 does not say. Presented with a route that improved on Route 894 by five habitable structures, the routing analysis traded those five structures against paralleling performance and preferred the route with more structures. That may well be a defensible judgment. But it is a weighting, an exchange rate between two criteria, and neither the finding nor the record states it. The same undisclosed exchange rate is what stands between Route 894 and every alternative in this proceeding, and Finding of Fact 160 presents its output as though it were a description of the routes rather than a product of an unstated method.
Requested relief. That Finding of Fact 160 be amended to state that Route 894 is one of several routes presenting an acceptable balance of routing factors, and that Conclusion of Law 16 be amended accordingly.
EXCEPTION 13: Proposed future development was given decisive weight in creating the route links and no weight in evaluating them.
At PFD 115, rejecting intervenors' future-development concerns, the ALJs state:
"The Commission has not afforded proposed future development in the same consideration as existing constraints. In Docket No. 55574, the Commission stated that it is 'not consistent with Commission precedent, in determining the best route, to give significant weight to the future development plans of some intervenors over existing constraints.' That standard defeated the Solana Intervenors, BOHKERS, and Whitis Land Investments.
Applicants applied no such standard to their own routing. The Environmental Assessment's "Table 6-1: Summary of Preliminary Route Link Additions and Removals" states, at the Figure 6-5 entry:
"Link F03 was added as continuation of the modified Link F0 (see Figure 6-34) that would parallel the proposed Corridor J transportation alignment. Links F04 and F20 were added as recommended alternatives to the original Link F0 and F2. Links F04 and F20 were provided as alternatives avoiding a large-scale proposed development between FM 2843 and a potential future highway.

Three things follow from that entry, and Applicants wrote all three.
First, Link F20 did not exist when the public meetings were held. It was added afterward, and its addition "splits Link F2 into Links F22 and F23, and Link F3 into Links F32 and F33." The link on which Mr. Howton's property sits, and the link the ALJs' recommended route uses, are both post-meeting creations.
Second, the stated reason for creating Link F20 was to avoid a proposed development and a potential future highway. Not to avoid habitable structures, not to reduce environmental impact, and not in response to any comment received at a meeting Mr. Howton's community was invited to.
Third, the development is named, and naming it is what exposes how little was behind it. The Environmental Assessment describes it only as "a large-scale proposed development between FM 2843 and a potential future highway." Applicants identified it in discovery:
"The proposed development is the Solana Development, and the potential future highway is Corridor J. Applicants do not know the name of the developer."
Mr. Marusak confirmed the identification on cross-examination.
Mr. Howton then asked what was known about the development that justified moving a 765-kV corridor for it. Specifically, whether as of the date Link F20 was added to the routing study the Solana Development had (a) an approved preliminary or final plat, (b) any building, grading, or infrastructure permits, (c) any state or federal regulatory approval, or (d) begun construction. The answer was:
"Applicants do not have responsive information."
And when asked to identify the routing criterion or factor weighting under which an unpermitted proposed development was treated as a constraint, Applicants cited only the general statutory list and added that they "consider planned development in conjunction with other existing constraints during route link development in an attempt to moderate impacts."
That is the whole of the record support. Applicants do not know the developer's name. They hold no document showing a plat, a permit, an approval, or construction. They identify no criterion authorizing the weighting. The standard the ALJs applied to intervenors at page 115, that future development counts only if "initiated in some readily observable or measurable way," was satisfied here by nothing at all. It nonetheless moved the line.
The same unbuilt highway shaped the surrounding links. Link F03 was added to "parallel the proposed Corridor J transportation alignment"; Links F01 and F34 were each "modified to better align with the proposed Corridor J transportation alignment"; and Link F05 was developed "with the intent to continue paralleling the future Corridor J transportation alignment."
Corridor J's own status is in evidence. Howton Exhibit JAH-21, the Halff Associates Corridor J3 engineering contract with Williamson County, was admitted. Applicants' own produced correspondence describes the corridor's posture as of September 2025: Corridor J "is included in [Williamson County's] Long Range Transportation Plan. There is not a formal roadway/project name yet. Preliminary engineering work has been funded and is being done. "All three segment studies are funded for study; however, no ROW or construction funding has been identified for any of the segments at this time."
And the record shows how Link F20 came to exist. Applicants produced, in response to Mr. Howton's discovery, a nine-page email chain of September 9–10, 2025 between counsel for the Solana stakeholders and Applicants' counsel. Its author records that Applicants asked for them: "As part of our conversation, as you may recall, you asked that the Solana stakeholders consider an alternate alignment to 'get to the north.' A4 and A5 are meant to show two ways to accomplish that."

Then the two answers that decide the point. Tr. Vol. 4 at 63:
Q. You didn't give us a formal notice — on the public meetings?
A. (Marusak) You did not get a notice on the public meetings because it was developed after —
Q. Would you agree that the F20 landowners were not afforded the same opportunity to offer the alternate routes that [was] provided [to] Solana Development and Ranch in advance of the submission of the CCN?

That is Applicants' own routing witness conceding differential opportunity: one landowner was invited to propose alignments before the Application was filed, and the landowners who received the resulting alignment were not. This is the concrete content of the "asymmetry of input" the ALJs identified in Section VI and declined to reach.
Mr. Howton does not ask the Commission to disregard future development. He asks that the standard be applied evenhandedly. If a landowner's development plans cannot outweigh existing constraints unless initiated in a readily observable or measurable way, then a highway with no identified right-of-way funding and a development with no plat, no permit, and no identified developer cannot justify creating a new corridor across an existing community that was given no opportunity to respond.
And Link F20 is not the only instance. Table 6-1 records that Link F45 "was added to provide an alternative to the original Link F4 to avoid a planned development on Tracts 2628, 2629, and 2630." Applicants added links to avoid planned development twice in the same link group, and identified one of the developments by tract number.
Applicants invoked future development unilaterally and before the Application was filed, when no party could test it. Intervenors invoked it on the record, under oath, and were told it does not count.

K. Link F20 was added after the public participation meetings as an alternative avoiding a proposed development and a potential future highway.
L. The Corridor J transportation alignment has no identified right-of-way or construction funding.
