C. Community Values
A note on what the comparative routing data measures
Several of the exceptions that follow share a premise, stated here once.
The routing tables compare alternative routes on counts: habitable structures within 500 feet, recorded cultural resource sites, miles across designated endangered or threatened species habitat, registered airports and airstrips. Each count is accurate as to what was identified. None measures what is present on the ground. Each measures what someone identified, recorded, or registered, and each therefore depends on who had the opportunity and the time to do so.
The Proposal for Decision establishes that the opportunity was not evenly distributed. Applicants mailed 2,809 invitations to the June 2025 public participation meetings. Finding of Fact 16. After those meetings Applicants added approximately 400 miles of route links, bringing roughly 1,400 additional landowners within the class entitled to notice and raising the affected class from roughly 2,800 to roughly 4,200. Findings of Fact 22, 27. None of those later-affected landowners was invited to a public meeting. Findings of Fact 24, 25. For those links, "no property owner (some 1,400) was able to identify routing constraints or address concerns at a public meeting, to their prejudice." Finding of Fact 26.
The consequence is not that the counts are unreliable at random. They are incomplete in a direction the record identifies. Constraints are reported more completely on links that existed nine months before the Application was filed than on links created afterward.
Mr. Howton's primary position remains that the Application should be denied on both grounds the ALJs identified. He adds that where the record establishes that comparative data was gathered unevenly, and identifies the direction, the evidence does not support the comparative determination among routes that PURA § 37.056(c)(4) and 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B) contemplate. That is a further reason to deny.
Should the Commission select a route notwithstanding, the direction of the defect bears on the selection. By centerline mileage, Route 894 is composed of post-meeting links to approximately six times the degree Route 296 is. See Exception 25.
EXCEPTION 14: The routing-criteria data reflects an asymmetry of landowner input that tracks the notice failure found in Findings of Fact 22 through 30.
This exception carries forward Exception 6.
The ALJs found that Applicants' post-meeting link modifications brought approximately 1,400 additional landowners within the affected class; that none was invited to a public participation meeting; and that this produced an "asymmetry of input."
The record confirms both that the mechanism works and that it was available only to those with notice and time:
• Applicants' witness Marusak testified that Salado Bluffs Airport, registered with the FAA one week before the Application was filed, came to Applicants' attention "very, very late," and that had they known, they would have "analyzed the links differently." PFD at 133–34.
• Landowners identified habitable structures that Applicants' methodology missed on Links U8, G51, and J22. PFD at 144–46. A further habitable structure was established on Link F20. Howton Ex. JAH-11; Tr. Vol. 4 at 52.
• The Roses obtained a Texas Historical Commission trinomial for the Taylor-Rose Ranch on Link G6. PFD at 122.
Mr. Howton does not suggest that any of those identifications was improper. Each was proper, and together they demonstrate precisely what the public participation meeting exists to accomplish. The point is the converse: the approximately 1,400 landowners never invited to a meeting had no comparable opportunity, and the comparative tables cannot be read as though they did.
Requested relief. A finding of fact that:
M. The routing-criteria data reflects constraints identified by Applicants and by landowners who received public-meeting notice, and does not reflect property-specific constraints on land brought within the affected class by the post-meeting link modifications.
And that Finding of Fact 176 be amended for consistency with Findings of Fact 25, 26, and 29, which establish that a substantial share of affected owners had no meeting at which to express community values.
1. Florence Elementary School
EXCEPTION 15: The ALJs disqualified Route 296 on a defect the record shows to be curable.
The ALJs' routing recommendation is Section VIII.L, at PFD 147 through 148. It is set out in full below, because the structure of the passage is what this exception addresses:
"The ALJs did not find cost to be a distinguishing factor in selecting a route, since the range of costs for the routes was in a relatively tight range. Similarly, the lengths among the Focus Routes are also comparable.
Ultimately, every Focus Route has its advantages and disadvantages. While Routes 296 and 392 perform favorably on environmental considerations because they utilize a Colorado River crossing with a pre-existing infrastructure corridor, they each have considerable downsides. The centerline of Route 296 runs within 500 feet of Florence Elementary School and two churches. Route 392 has notably more habitable structures and cultural resources on it than other Focus Routes. As such, the ALJs find that Routes 487 and 894 achieve prudent avoidance more effectively than Routes 296 and 392.
In comparing the Central Corridor routes (Routes 487 and 894), Route 487 has the highest percentage parallelling compatible ROW but also has the largest impact on parks and recreational areas of the Focus Routes. Route 487 is the only Focus Route that runs within 1,000 feet of a park or recreational area and has substantially more miles within the half-mile foreground visual zone of park and recreational areas. Conversely, no part of Route 894's centerline runs within 1,000 feet of the parks or recreational areas or is within the half-mile foreground visual zone of park and recreational areas. Route 894 performs favorably on habitable structures, paralleling existing compatible ROW, crossing rangeland pasture, and crossing riparian areas.
And still, Route 894 would be visible from many areas of Colorado Bend State Park and Post Oak Ridge State Park and intersects a private grass airstrip. The ALJs are tasked with choosing the least bad option available based on consideration of the routing factors. Therefore, if any route must be chosen, the ALJs recommend selection of Route 894."
Cost does not distinguish the routes. Length does not distinguish them. Route 296 performs favorably on environmental considerations. Route 392's downside is stated as a comparative count: it "has notably more habitable structures and cultural resources on it than other Focus Routes." Route 296's downside is stated differently. It is not a count. It is three named structures. That difference in method is what this exception addresses.
Two further features of the passage bear on exceptions that follow. The ALJs credit Route 894 for "paralleling existing compatible ROW," which is the figure Exception 21 shows to be composed 93.6% of apparent property boundaries and last among the routes compared. And the ALJs record that Route 894 "intersects a private grass airstrip," which is Salado Bluffs Airport and is the subject of Exception 20. Neither observation appears in any finding of fact.
The Proposal for Decision applies two different measures to the two routes.
For Route 894, the habitable-structure count is the measure. Finding of Fact 167 states that Route 894 "has 85 known habitable structures located within 500 feet of its centerline." Finding of Fact 168 concludes, on that basis and no other, that Route 894 "complies with the Commission's policy of prudent avoidance."
For Route 296, the count is not the measure. Its count of 105 does not decide it. The passage at PFD 147 rests the conclusion on three named structures: Florence Elementary School and two churches.
Those are two different methods, applied to two routes, in the same section of the same document, producing opposite results. Under Rule 22.262(a)(1)(A) that is a failure to apply the Commission's rule consistently.
And the choice of those three structures is difficult to reconcile with the standard Finding of Fact 166 recites. Prudent avoidance limits exposures. A school is occupied on school days during school hours; a church is occupied for services. Of the categories in Applicants' own structure-type table at PFD 144, those are the categories least continuously occupied. On the rule's own measure, the three structures the ALJs singled out are the three least exposure-intensive of Route 296's 105.
Mr. Howton asks the Commission to draw no conclusion about the relative worth of a school, a church, or a home, and takes no position that any structure deserves less protection than any other. Rule 25.101(a)(3) lists churches and schools as habitable structures alongside dwellings and draws no distinction among them, and Mr. Howton proposes none. The point is narrower and is about the Proposal for Decision, not about the structures: the ALJs cannot both rest Route 894's compliance on the aggregate count and rest Route 296's rejection on three structures the aggregate count does not distinguish. One measure must govern both routes.
Either the three carry weight beyond their number in the count, in which case the count is not the measure of prudent avoidance and Finding of Fact 168 does not follow for Route 894; or they do not, in which case three structures out of 105 cannot be the stated ground for rejecting Route 296.
And the factors that do distinguish the two routes favor Route 296.

Route 296 parallels existing compatible rights-of-way for 38,612 more feet, or 7.31 more miles, than Route 894. More to the point, and on the measure the ALJs recorded as "a more appropriate comparison" and then applied in their own voice, Route 296 parallels more than twice as much existing electric transmission line and more than three times as much public roadway as Route 894, for a combined 26.60 miles against 10.11. Route 894's larger-sounding total is composed 93.6% of apparent property boundaries, which Commission Staff witness Poole testified are "less reliable than both paralleling transmission lines and roadways." Route 296 also crosses one quarter as much federally listed species habitat, and crosses less riparian area and less high-potential archeological terrain. Route 894 leads on habitable structures by 20, on recorded cultural resources, on stream crossings, and on cost by 0.22%.
The habitable-structure difference is the one Applicants and the ALJs rely on, and it is the least durable number in the table. Cherokee Creek witness Reinecke testified that the standard deviation across the filed routes' counts is approximately 27 structures; the difference here is 20, inside one standard deviation. The counts are also demonstrably incomplete: the record establishes structures omitted from the counts on Links U8, G51, J22, and F20. A twenty-structure difference derived from a count with a twenty-seven-structure standard deviation and known omissions cannot outweigh 7.31 miles of additional paralleling and a fourfold difference in endangered-species habitat, each of which is a separate statutory criterion.
Mr. Howton does not contend that Route 296 prevails on every factor. He contends that the balance PURA § 37.056(c)(4) requires was not struck, because the one factor on which Route 894 leads was treated as decisive without regard to its margin of error, and the factors on which Route 296 leads were not weighed against it at all.
All three structures are on Link F34, and Applicants' own errata says so. On June 1, 2026, Applicants filed a Notice of Errata reclassifying four habitable structures that Table 7-5 had described as "Commercial/Industrial." As revised, the entries read:

Structure 458 is not on Route 296. It sits on Link F8, and Route 296's link sequence does not include Link F8. Mr. Howton identifies it here so that the Commission has the complete set of reclassified structures before it, and so that no party can suggest the exception was built by selecting only the favorable three.
The three structures the ALJs identified at PFD 147 are therefore structures 354, 303, and 304, all on Link F34, at 395, 430, and 360 feet. One link carries the entire stated ground for rejecting Route 296.
The distances matter as much as the link. None of the three is at the margin. Each sits between 360 and 430 feet from a centerline whose governing threshold is 500 feet. The adjustment required to place all three outside 500 feet is on the order of 70 to 140 feet, before any allowance for the 520-foot identification buffer Applicants used. This is not a route that must be abandoned to protect a school. It is an alignment that must move the width of a fence line.
That ground is curable, and five things in the record establish it.
First, Rule 22.52(a)(3)(D) requires modification notice only to landowners "who have not already received notice." A within-tract adjustment that stays on already-noticed tracts raises no notice defect under the rule's own terms.
Second, the ALJs have already accepted the principle. At PFD 37: "The ALJs agree that assembling routes from previously noticed links does not itself create a notice defect."
Third, Applicants' witness testified that a utility may make a minor adjustment to mitigate potential impact to a structure.
Fourth, and most concretely, Link F34 has already been adjusted once. The Environmental Assessment records that "Link F34 was modified to better align with the proposed Corridor J transportation alignment." Applicants also developed and then abandoned Link F05 in this same link group to avoid a conservation easement. Applicants adjust links in this area as a matter of course, and did so to avoid an easement.
Fifth, the geometry permits it, and Applicants' own notice table proves every element. The tract Link F34 crosses at this location is Tract 2361. Applicants' own list of landowners to whom Application notice was mailed identifies it:

Three things follow from that table alone, without any evidence outside the record:
1. Tract 2361's owner received Application notice. It is on Applicants' own notice list. An adjustment confined to that tract therefore requires notice to no landowner who has not already received it. 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(3)(D).
2. Tract 2361 carries no habitable structure. The "habitable structures" column is blank for Tract 2361, as it is for Tracts 2360 and 2364. The only tract in this group carrying a habitable structure is Tract 2362, and the structure is number 354, Florence Elementary School itself, on the school district's own land.
3. The school is on the adjoining tract to the south. The alignment is on the southern edge of Tract 2361; the school district's tract adjoins that edge. Moving the alignment north within Tract 2361 moves it away from the school, not toward it.
What makes this tract remarkable is what surrounds it. Three of its four boundaries are existing state highway right-of-way.

Tract 2361 sits within the block formed by SH 195 on the east, SH 138 across the north, and Business SH 195 on the west, north of Florence. Its western boundary is not a straight property line but the curve of the former highway alignment. Its only boundary that is not a highway is the southern one, and that is the boundary the school adjoins.
Applicants routed along the school side. Across Tract 2361 the Link F34 centerline runs near the tract's southern boundary, which is the only side of the tract with no highway on it and the side the school adjoins. The tract's northern boundary, along SH 138, lies substantially farther from the school than the current centerline does. Mr. Howton does not ask the Commission to find any particular distance. The configuration is what matters, and it appears on the face of the admitted aerial imagery.
The alignment is not incidental to that boundary. It parallels it. Across Tract 2361 the Link F34 centerline runs close to, and on essentially the same bearing as, the tract's southern property line, the one boundary of the tract that is not a highway right-of-way, and it is that placement, rather than anything about the tract itself, that brings the centerline within 500 feet of the school and the two churches on the adjoining tracts to the south. The tract, the alignment across it, the school on the adjoining tract, and the surrounding highway network are all shown in the aerial imagery admitted as Yates Keith Alliance Exhibit 14. Applicants' witness Marusak confirmed on cross-examination that the imagery is consistent with what he observed on his own site visit, and that the school structure shown in it "should be where we would have measured to."
That is a routing choice with a name in this record. Applicants aligned the link to parallel an apparent property boundary, the category Commission Staff witness Poole testified is "less reliable than both paralleling transmission lines and roadways." The same bearing, carried across the northern portion of the same tract, would have paralleled the state highway right-of-way along that tract's northern boundary, the category the routing criteria actually favor, and would have placed the centerline substantially farther from the school than 395 feet. Applicants chose the weaker form of paralleling, and that choice is what places the centerline where it is.
This is Exception 21's defect reduced to a single tract. Route 894 reports 484,456 feet of paralleling of apparent property boundaries and only 23,498 feet of paralleling of public roads and highways. Tract 2361 shows how a ratio like that is produced: given a tract bounded by highway on three sides and a property line on the fourth, the routing study followed the property line.
An adjustment to the northern boundary would accomplish two things at once, each of which the Commission's criteria favor:
1. It would move the alignment substantially farther from Florence Elementary School and from the two church structures, and would place all three beyond the 500-foot distance the habitable-structure criterion measures.
2. It would place the alignment alongside an existing highway right-of-way, the outcome most favored by 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B)(ii).
Neither requires notice to any landowner who has not already received it, because the adjustment stays within a tract Applicants already cross and whose owner is on their own notice list.
Route 894 parallels public roads and highways for 23,498 feet across its entire 223 miles. Route 296 parallels 78,378 feet. Here, on a tract the routing study was already crossing, with a state highway along its northern boundary and two more along the east and west, the alignment was placed on the one boundary with no roadway at all, and against a school. The record does not show that any highway-adjacent alternative on this tract was considered.
The chronology is in the Proposal for Decision, and it belongs in the findings. At PFD 109–11 the ALJs record each of the following:
• Florence Elementary School opened in August 2025 and serves approximately 530 students.
• Applicants' routing consultants wrote to Florence ISD Superintendent Dr. Rick Kirkpatrick on January 24, 2025, informing the district of the Project.
• Applicants' witness Marusak physically visited the property in June 2025 and confirmed the presence of the school.
• The Application nonetheless "erroneously identified the school as a habitable structure, when it should have also been identified as an elementary school," a classification corrected only by errata filed June 1, 2026, one week before the hearing.
• "Applicants typically coordinate with all the school districts about the project and help in identifying locations of interest within their district, but this did not happen with Florence ISD."
• Applicants "do not 'want to route any components of the school building, playground areas, those types of locations that would be within the right-of-way.'"
• Florence Elementary School "is located approximately 395 feet from the centerline of Link F34."
Applicants knew about this school nine months before they filed. Their witness stood on the property in June 2025 and confirmed it. They had written to the superintendent five months before that. They did not coordinate with the district, did not consult the Texas Education Agency or the Department of Health and Human Services after learning the school's location, and were "not aware of any long-term effects on the health and safety of elementary school students from transmission lines in proximity to the campus nor did they consult any studies to that effect."
And one further fact makes the curability question decisive. Staff witness Poole "initially stated in deposition that Route 296 was Staff's second favorite route. However, after further evidence was produced, Staff no longer considers Route 296 second place." The evidence that moved Staff off Route 296 is the school. The feature that cost Route 296 its standing with the Commission's own Staff is the feature Exception 15 shows to be curable by an adjustment within a tract Applicants already cross, on a bearing Applicants already use, toward a highway Applicants already parallel elsewhere.
Increased road paralleling is a second, independent gain. Whether routes "parallel or utilize other existing compatible rights-of-way, including roads, highways, railroads, or telephone utility rights-of-way" is a factor the Commission must consider. An adjustment that moves the alignment onto the northern boundary of Tract 2361 alongside an existing roadway would increase that percentage while simultaneously increasing separation from the school. Applicants' own description of Link F34 locates the link by reference to the highways that bound this tract: this segment of Link F34 "crosses N Patterson Ave, South Salado Creek, and SH 195, approximately 1,160 feet southeast from the intersection of SH 195 and SH 138, north of Florence, Texas." The adjacency of the highway right-of-way to the northern boundary of the tract, and of the school to the tract immediately south, appears on the face of the admitted aerial imagery.
Applicants adjust links to increase distance from sensitive uses as a matter of routine. Table 6-2 records that Link B3 was modified "to increase distance from a habitable structure"; Link E2 "to increase distance from habitable structures"; Link G31 "to increase distance from a fire station helipad"; Link M12 "to decrease the impact to The Ranches at Buck Ridge subdivision"; and Link M32 was shifted in a manner that "also reduced the potential impact to a commercial bird raising facility." Applicants also abandoned Link F05 entirely after the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service verified that portions of it crossed the Pecan Springs Karst Preserve, describing that decision as "[c]onsistent with other routing modifications described in Table 6-1 and Table 6-2 to avoid these areas." Link F34 was itself modified once, "to better align with the proposed Corridor J transportation alignment." It was not modified to increase distance from the school or the churches, and the record does not show that any such adjustment was considered.
Applicants' own conduct as to the school is the weakest part of their routing case. The ALJs found that Applicants "typically coordinate with all the school districts about the project ... but this did not happen with Florence ISD"; that after learning of the school they did not consult the Texas Education Agency or the Department of Health and Human Services; and that witness Marusak testified "All things being equal ... if I can avoid a school, I'm certainly going to look to."
Finally, Applicants have themselves argued that proximity of approximately 395 feet to a school "provides no basis to reject the link," citing Docket No. 51023, and have conceded that a 500-foot count "should not be a thoughtless mathematical exercise." Both propositions cut against them. If 395 feet does not disqualify a link, the school cannot be the sole reason to reject Route 296. If the 500-foot count is not a thoughtless mathematical exercise, Route 894's count of 85 cannot carry the weight Findings of Fact 167 and 168 place on it.
Disclosure regarding Link F34. The record contains a separate question about this link. Intervenor Kevin Kennedy asserts that Applicants failed to consider Williamson County's proposed five-level interchange at SH 195 and Corridor J on Link F34; Commission Staff witness Poole did not recall seeing in the Application that Link F34 went through the middle of a five-level interchange, said that is information he would want to know, and did not dispute that vertical clearance was a potential issue with the 198-foot maximum height lattice tower Applicants propose. Mr. Howton raises the point himself because an exception asking the Commission to adjust a link should account for what else is known about that link.
Mr. Howton does not ask the Commission to find that Route 296's habitable-structure count would change. He asks only that the three structures the ALJs identified would no longer lie within 500 feet of the centerline.
Nor does he ask the Commission to find the adjustment feasible or cost-justified, and the distinction disposes of Applicants' authority. Applicants rely on Application of LCRA Transmission Services Corporation to Amend a Certificate of Convenience and Necessity for the Round Rock–Leander 138-kV Transmission Line in Williamson County, Docket No. 45866, Order on Rehearing, Findings of Fact 49–50 (July 28, 2017), where the Commission rejected a school district's request to modify a route for deeper setbacks because the record contained no evidence that the proposed modification was feasible or cost justified. Mr. Howton does not ask for the finding that was missing there. He does not ask the Commission to order an alignment, to find a shift feasible, or to price one.
He asks for something narrower and different in kind: that the Commission decline to treat the school and church proximities as a fixed and disqualifying attribute of Route 296, when the record shows the link crosses a tract that carries no habitable structure, whose owner already received notice of the Application, and that adjoins a state highway right-of-way on its northern boundary. Whether a particular alignment within that tract is workable is a field question, and the Commission has a mechanism for field questions that it adopted one week before this filing: the landowner-consent deviation paragraph described in Exception 31. That paragraph defers feasibility to the parties who can actually determine it, on consent, without a further amendment. Docket No. 45866 holds that a setback cannot be ordered on a silent record. It does not hold that a curable proximity must be treated as permanent.
Mr. Howton does not suggest that every defect in this record is curable, and the distinction is not a convenient one. The notice failure the ALJs found is not curable, for the reasons given at Exceptions 2 and 3: it would require a public meeting that can no longer be held within the period PURA § 37.057 allows, for a class of roughly 1,400 owners, and the day-for-day extension the rule provides has nothing left to extend. The Link F34 proximity is curable for the opposite reason. It requires no meeting, no additional notice, and no additional time, because the adjustment stays within a tract Applicants already cross and whose owner is already on their notice list. One defect needs a process that is closed. The other needs a fence line.
A conflict in the record on the school's distance, which Mr. Howton flags rather than exploits. Certain intervenors state that Link F34 "would bring the 765-kV transmission line within approximately 200 feet of Florence Elementary School." Applicants' errata'd Table 7-5 gives 395 feet. The figures are reconcilable and measure different things: 395 feet is the distance from the school structure to the link centerline, which is what Rule 22.52(a)(3) and the habitable-structure criterion measure, while the Florence ISD tract boundary lies substantially closer to the centerline than the building does. Mr. Howton uses Applicants' own 395-foot figure throughout, because it is the figure the routing criteria actually turn on. Whichever measure the Commission prefers, the direction of the cure is the same and the magnitude of the available shift is unchanged.

E. Aesthetic and Historic Values
EXCEPTION 16: The cultural-resource counts measure recorded sites only, and no finding says so.
The Combined Data Table reports "recorded cultural resource sites," meaning sites bearing a Texas Historical Commission designation. Whether a site is recorded reflects landowner initiative, resources, and time, not whether the site exists.
The PFD documents that mechanism operating during this proceeding: the Roses established Trinomial 41BT562 on Link G6 (Route 296); Kat Brown "is in the process of registering" her family property on Links G51 and G52 (Routes 392 and 487); and Soldier's Hole on Link J6 (Route 296), though locally recognized, bears no marker. Applicants' witness Marusak "acknowledged that just because the area has not been formally identified as historically significant does not mean that it is insignificant or should be ignored."
The Rose/Joppa 1886 Trust further established that Applicants failed to identify the Taylor-Rose Ranch's cultural designation on the Amended Combined Data Table at all. That is not a dispute about significance. It is an omission from the table on which the comparison rests.
The comparative claim that carries this section is not in a finding of fact. At PFD 122 the ALJs write that "Route 894 has 12 cultural resource sites within 1,000 feet of its centerline, tied for the lowest number of any filed route," citing App. Ex. 23. Findings of Fact 198 through 201 contain no such comparison. Finding of Fact 199 recites the bare number, "There are 12 recorded cultural sites located with 1,000 feet of Route 894's centerline," and Finding of Fact 201 concludes that Route 894 "minimizes impacts to historical and archeological resources to a reasonable extent." The step between them, the comparison to other routes, appears only in the narrative.
Two qualifications belong in the record on that comparison.
First, "tied for the lowest" describes a tie among 16 of the 122 filed routes, all of which report 12. App. Ex. 1, att. 11 (Routing Memorandum), Table 2, row "Number of recorded cultural resources within 1,000 feet of the route centerline." A metric on which one-eighth of the filed routes share the minimum does not distinguish Route 894 from the alternatives.
Second, on the companion metric, recorded sites crossed, Route 894 crosses two, and the minimum among filed routes is zero. App. Ex. 1, att. 11 (Routing Memorandum), Table 2, row "Number of recorded cultural resource sites crossed by the route"; PFD FoF 198. Route 894 is not lowest on that measure.
The second metric does not depend on registration, and it points the other way. The Environmental Assessment models areas of high potential for historical or archeological sites from geomorphology. That measure does not depend on whether a landowner filed anything. Finding of Fact 200 states that Route 894 "crosses areas with high potential for historical or archeological sites for 54.34 miles, or 24.3% of its length." The comparative figures appear at PFD 102:

Route 894 crosses more high-potential area than Route 296. The margin is 1.35 miles, and Route 487 is lower than either at 50.56 miles. Mr. Howton does not present this as a large difference or as a ground for preferring Route 296 standing alone. He presents it because the two metrics point in opposite directions, and the record explains why: one counts designations, and the other does not.
The record also shows how a designation comes to be recorded, and how it does not. A cultural resource within 1,000 feet of Link F20, a link added after the June 2025 public participation meetings, was identified and tendered on June 7, 2026, the day before the hearing on the merits opened. The ALJs took the notice up on the opening morning of the hearing, read it as seeking admission of Exhibit AEH-27 "to identify the location of First Cedar Valley Baptist Church," and directed that the evidence be placed in the record "either through cross-examination or a stipulation from the Applicants." The exhibit was not thereafter offered, and it is not in evidence.
The timing of that offer is not incidental, and it illustrates the asymmetry found at Finding of Fact 26. Landowners on links that existed before the June 2025 public meetings had those meetings, and then roughly nine months before the Application was filed, in which to identify constraints on their land and to seek out whatever expertise those constraints called for. Landowners on Link F20 had neither, because Link F20 did not exist until September 22, 2025, three months after the last meeting and six months before filing.
The consequence is visible in the shape of the cultural record for this link. What the Commission has before it on Link F20 is a landowner's testimony about a National Register site a few miles upstream, offered by a resident of twenty-two years rather than by an archaeologist, and a notice of a cultural resource tendered on the eve of the hearing. Mr. Howton does not offer that as an excuse and does not ask the Commission to receive evidence that is not properly before it. He offers it as the answer to an argument Applicants may make: that the thinness of the cultural record for Link F20 shows there is little there. It shows something different. It shows that the people best positioned to identify what is there were brought into the process after the point at which the rule contemplates their participation, which is what Finding of Fact 26 found and what Exception 3 addresses.
The ruling was correct, and its uniformity is the point. The ALJs applied the same direction that same morning to Mr. Howton's own notice of an unidentified habitable structure, reading it as seeking admission of his exhibit "to show a habitable structure that is missing from Applicants' environmental assessment" and directing that the evidence be put in "either through cross-examination or a stipulation on the record with the Applicants." Mr. Howton did that, and Exhibit JAH-11 was admitted. Mr. Howton does not except to any evidentiary ruling and does not ask the Commission to reconsider one; Rule 22.123(a)(1) forecloses that in terms: "Appeals are not available for evidentiary rulings. Interim orders are not subject to exceptions or motions for rehearing."
What the two rulings show is not disparate treatment. It is the difference between the two kinds of proof. A landowner can establish a missing habitable structure on cross-examination with a photograph and a map, because the fact is visible from the road and the witness has driven the road. A landowner cannot establish an archaeological site that way. Identifying what lies beneath a corridor takes a survey and an expert, and the public participation process is where the Commission's rules contemplate that a landowner learns to go looking. Owners on links that existed before the June 2025 meetings had that process and the nine months that followed it. Owners on Link F20 had neither.
He asks the Commission to notice only what the sequence shows about the comparison. The ALJs wrote that procedural rules "neutral in themselves, fell hardest on the unrepresented landowners who had the least time to intervene, retain counsel, and convert their concerns into admissible evidence rather than protests." Landowners on links that existed nine months before filing had the public participation process and the full procedural schedule in which to identify and document constraints, and the Proposal for Decision credits three cultural resources they identified. A landowner on a link created after that process had neither. The cultural-resource comparison reflects the difference, and no finding says so.
Mr. Howton notes for completeness that the ALJs granted his own motion to supplement the record after the hearing. That motion concerned discovery responses Applicants served at 2:36 p.m. on June 9 while the hearing was underway, as the Proposal for Decision records at n.198. The distinction is not that one party was favored. It is that a party may cure a late discovery production and cannot cure a public meeting that was never held.
No finding addresses what either metric measures.
Requested relief. Findings of fact that:
N. The cultural-resource counts reflect only sites recorded with the Texas Historical Commission; the record establishes sites of historical significance that are unrecorded, and at least one recorded designation omitted from the Amended Combined Data Table. Twelve recorded sites within 1,000 feet is the minimum value reported among the filed routes, shared by 16 of the 122 filed routes.
W. Route 894 crosses 54.34 miles of areas identified in the Environmental Assessment as having high potential for historical or archeological sites. Route 296 crosses 52.99 miles and Route 487 crosses 50.56 miles. That measure does not depend on whether a site has been recorded with the Texas Historical Commission.
Disclosure. The Taylor-Rose Ranch lies on Link G6, which is a link of Route 296. Correcting the Amended Combined Data Table to reflect Trinomial 41BT562 would therefore increase Route 296's recorded-site count, not Route 894's. Mr. Howton raises the omission because it establishes that the table is incomplete, and the incompleteness runs against the route he prefers as readily as against Route 894. The point is the reliability of the metric, not the direction of a particular correction.
And the same defect produced the reported figure on Link F20. On cross-examination, Applicants' witness Marusak confirmed that the cultural resources review for Link F20 rested on the Texas Historical Commission's recorded-site database desktop review; that Table 7-3 reports Link F20 crossing approximately 3,831 feet of high archaeological or historical site potential; that the same table reports zero recorded cultural resource sites crossing Link F20; and that no field archaeological survey of the F20 corridor was conducted before the route was selected. Asked whether the high-potential designation exists precisely because such corridors are known to contain deeply buried deposits that a desktop database review cannot detect, he agreed.
A zero produced by a desktop review of recorded sites, across a link with thousands of feet of modeled high potential and no field survey, is not evidence that nothing is there. It is the same artifact that omitted Trinomial 41BT562 from the Amended Combined Data Table, appearing this time on a link of the recommended route. The metric under-reports in both directions, which is why it cannot discriminate between these routes and why the companion finding requested below is necessary.
What the zero on Link F20 omits is a matter of record. Mr. Howton testified:
"The Gault Archaeological Site, also known as part of the Buttermilk Creek Complex, is located a few miles west of my property upstream Buttermilk Creek in Bell County. It is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. Archaeological research at the site, conducted in part by Texas A&M University's Center for the Study of the First Americans, has documented human occupation extending back at least 20,000 years, placing the Gault Site among the most significant pre-Columbian archaeological sites in North America.
Link F20 crosses the Buttermilk Creek watershed. I have lived in this community for 22 years and have direct knowledge of the Gault Site's location and significance. Based on my review of the Applicants' Environmental Assessment and routing materials, I have not been able to locate any discussion of the Gault Archaeological Site in connection with the proposed corridor."
Applicants' witness Marusak did not dispute the point when it was put to him; asked whether he was aware that the Buttermilk Creek complex within the F20 study area is among the oldest documented human habitation sites in North America, he answered that he was "not aware of the specifics, but … aware of a lot of archeological sites in this part of the study area."
That is the whole difficulty with the metric, expressed in a single link. The Application reports Link F20 as crossing zero recorded cultural resource sites while crossing approximately 3,831 feet of terrain modeled as having high potential for such sites. Both numbers are correct. Together they say that the corridor runs through ground the model flags as likely to contain buried deposits, and that nobody has looked. A transmission corridor crossing the Buttermilk Creek watershed downstream of a National Register site with 20,000 years of documented occupation is recorded in the comparative tables as a zero, indistinguishable from a link crossing ground of no archaeological interest whatever.
Deeply buried Paleoindian deposits are, by definition, not visible from the surface and not in a recorded-site database until someone excavates. That is precisely why the high-potential designation exists, a proposition Applicants' own witness accepted when it was put to him. The zero is therefore not a finding of absence. It is a record of the fact that no survey was performed.
Mr. Howton does not ask the Commission to find that any artifact exists beneath Link F20. He asks it to decline to treat a desktop zero as though it were a survey result, and to make the companion finding below so that the comparative tables are read for what they measure. The prospective protection he requests, applicable to whichever route is approved, is at Exception 29.
F. Environmental Integrity
EXCEPTION 17: The endangered species metric measures critical habitat designation rather than habitat, and Route 894 is highest among the Focus Routes on the metric as reported.
The reported figure for Link F20 was not derived from any survey of Link F20. Applicants' witness Marusak agreed on cross-examination that no site-specific field survey of Golden-cheeked warbler habitat was conducted on Link F20, and that the zero-acreage endangered-species figure reported for that link "reflects a GIS overlay of the U.S. Fish & Wildlife designated critical habitat boundaries, not a field survey." Per Applicants' Resp. to Howton RFI Set No. 2, No. 1-65, field environmental surveys will be performed only after the Commission selects a route.
Applicants treated the same constraint differently on a different link. Mr. Marusak confirmed that Link F05 was developed and then removed from consideration after Applicants validated with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service that it crossed a karst preserve. Where the constraint was identified before filing, Applicants met with the Service and deleted the link. For Link F20, no survey will occur until after the route is selected. Asked about that asymmetry, Mr. Marusak narrowed rather than denied it: "we met with U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service to discuss several elements of the project area. But … there was one link that it was advised that we remove it."
A metric that records a designation rather than a condition, on a link never surveyed, cannot establish that the link is free of the habitat the criterion exists to protect.
The Environmental Assessment data reports the length of each route across federally listed endangered or threatened species habitat. PFD at 124:

Route 894 reports the highest figure of the four Focus Routes. No finding of fact records the comparison.
The record also establishes what the metric measures. Carpenter witness Aaron Brewer testified that "[t]he entire project corridor passes through core [golden-cheeked warbler] breeding range, [but] every route shows zero GCWA contribution to the threatened and endangered species impact criteria. . . . This lack of effect is not because GCWA habitat is absent, but because there is no formal critical habitat designation." Ms. Suzanne Thomson testified to documented golden-cheeked warbler sightings along the G51 and G52 corridor.
That is the same structure as the cultural-resource metric. The measure turns on a formal designation rather than on the presence of the resource, and every filed route reports zero contribution from a federally endangered species whose core breeding range the entire corridor occupies.
Disclosure, and a qualification the record requires. The Colorado River Alliance asserts that Link J31, a link of Route 296, is the only link known to cut through known and occupied golden-cheeked warbler habitat. Mr. Howton does not ask the Commission to disregard that assertion as to Link J31, and he does not contend that Route 296 is free of golden-cheeked warbler habitat.
He does not, however, accept the assertion in its exclusive form, because the record contains contrary evidence as to Link F20. Aaron Edward Howton, who holds a university degree in wildlife science, testified that he observed a golden-cheeked warbler on Tract 5645, within 500 feet of the proposed right-of-way on Link F20.
The two links illustrate the same defect from opposite directions, which is this exception's point. Link J31's habitat is "known" because it falls within a designation. Link F20's is not "known" in that sense because Applicants conducted no field survey there and relied on a GIS overlay of designated critical-habitat boundaries, as their witness confirmed. A metric that records designation rather than presence will report the surveyed link as carrying habitat and the unsurveyed link as carrying none, and will do so no matter which link the birds are actually on. Mr. Howton does not ask the Commission to resolve whether Link F20 contains occupied habitat. He asks it to recognize that the comparison between the two links is, in part, a comparison between a place that was examined and a place that was not. It is recorded here because the argument is about what the metric measures, and that argument does not become weaker when applied to the route he prefers.
Requested relief. A finding of fact that:
X. Route 894 crosses 0.09 miles of federally listed endangered or threatened species habitat, the highest figure among the Focus Routes. The record establishes that every filed route reports no golden-cheeked warbler contribution to the threatened and endangered species criteria, and that this reflects the absence of a formal critical habitat designation rather than the absence of habitat.

At PFD 124-25 the Proposal for Decision states that Applicants "had initially proposed Links K3, J2, J6, and J5 in the public meetings but they were not included in the filed Application," and quotes the Environmental Assessment for the proposition that "[t]hese links were removed due to significant environmental impacts."

G. Costs
EXCEPTION 19: The Proposal for Decision compares Route 296 to the wrong route, and overstates its cost disadvantage against Route 894 by a factor of approximately five.
At PFD 129 the ALJs write:
"Route 296's cost is $1.685 billion, which is $20 million (1.20%) more than Route 894."
Route 296 is not $20 million more than Route 894. It is $20 million more than Route 487, which is the subject of the sentence two sentences earlier.
The underlying figures are not in dispute. Findings of Fact 161 through 164 establish them: the 122 filed routes range from $1,636,232,000 to $1,857,768,000 excluding station costs; station costs are $395,468,000 regardless of route; Route 894 is $1,680,919,000 excluding station costs and $2,076,387,000 including them.
The per-route figures come from App. Ex. 1, att. 4 (Cost Estimates), at the row headed "Estimated Total Transmission Line Cost." That is the same attachment and the same row the ALJs cite.

The same figures appear in two later Applicant filings. Applicants' Notice of Routes of Interest Map and Combined Data Table, Item No. 5745 (June 3, 2026), Attachment A, gives the identical figure for every route above at its row "Estimated Transmission Line Cost" (Route 296 at page 46; Route 894 at page 131).
Four of these figures are independently corroborated by Applicants' errata. On June 1, 2026, Applicants filed a corrected version of the Routing Memorandum, Application Attachment No. 11. Its narrative states that "[t]he estimated transmission line cost for Route 894 is $1,680,919,000, which is 2.73% more than the least expensive transmission line cost (Route 469 estimated at $1,636,232,000)," and that Route 894 "is approximately 9.52% less costly than the filed route with the most expensive transmission line cost (Route 910 estimated at $1,857,768,000)." The same document's corridor summaries give the minimum transmission line cost of the Link J27 corridor as $1,658,694,000, the Link J24 corridor as $1,662,575,000, and the Link J32 corridor as $1,665,042,000, and the maximum of the Link J27 corridor as $1,842,214,000.
On those figures:

The difference the ALJs state, "$20 million," is $19,749,000 rounded. That is exactly Route 296 minus Route 487. The stated percentage is consistent with the same comparator: $20,000,000 against Route 487's $1,664,814,000 is 1.2013%, which is the "1.20%" in the text. Against Route 894 the same $20 million would be 1.19%, and the true delta of $3,644,000 would be 0.22%.
The most likely explanation is a carried-over comparator. The preceding sentence is about Route 487; the label changed and the baseline did not.
A related imprecision in the same paragraph. Mr. Howton does not except to the following, but notes it because the corrected figure should be read against a consistent basis. Within a single sentence the ALJs switch denominators:
"Staff's recommended Route 487 at $1.665 billion is only 1.41% more expensive than the cheapest route, and 0.95% cheaper than Route 894."
The first figure is computed on total project cost, including the $395,468,000 station cost: ($2,060,282,000 − $2,031,700,000) ÷ $2,031,700,000 = 1.4068%. On transmission-line cost alone the same comparison is 1.75%. The second figure is computed on transmission-line cost alone: ($1,680,919,000 − $1,664,814,000) ÷ $1,680,919,000 = 0.9581%. On total project cost the same comparison is 0.78%. The preceding sentence's "2.7% more than the cheapest route" is likewise computed on transmission-line cost (2.7311%), although its grammatical subject is Route 894's $2.076 billion total project cost.
The station cost is constant across routes, so the choice of denominator does not change any ranking. It changes only the apparent size of the gaps, and it does so inconsistently within one paragraph.
Cost is a routing consideration under 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B), which directs that a transmission line "must be routed to the extent reasonable to moderate the impact on the affected community and landowners unless grid reliability and security dictate otherwise," after addressing "the criteria in PURA §37.056(c) and considering those criteria, engineering constraints, and costs." The ALJs elsewhere relied on the closeness of the routes on cost, quoting Staff witness Poole that the costs "are 'in a tight range relative to what we see in some of these cases.'" PFD at 129. The corrected figure places Route 296 within approximately one-fifth of one percent of Applicants' preferred route, inside any reasonable estimating tolerance, and well inside the 10% to 15% contingency Applicants themselves applied.
Mr. Howton raises this as a correction, not as an argument that cost favors Route 296. It does not. It establishes that cost does not meaningfully distinguish the two routes at all.
One further figure, from the same table. Route 894 is not an inexpensive route. Of the 122 filed routes, 44 carry a lower estimated transmission line cost than Route 894, and 37 of those 44 avoid both Link F20 and Link F23. Mr. Howton does not contend that any of those 37 is the best-meets route; most are worse than Route 894 on habitable structures, and he takes no position on routes he has not analyzed. The figure bears on a narrower point: the ALJs declined to treat cost as a distinguishing factor because the routes sit in a tight range, and on Applicants' own data that tight range contains dozens of cheaper routes that do not use the two links at issue here. Cost cannot simultaneously be too tight to distinguish among routes and a reason to prefer the one Applicants chose.
Requested relief. That the sentence at PFD 129 be corrected to reflect that the $20 million difference is between Route 296 and Route 487, and findings of fact entered that:
U (already proposed; restated here for context). The estimated cost of Route 296 exceeds that of Route 894 by approximately $3.6 million, or approximately 0.22%, excluding station costs.
AH. Of the 122 filed routes, 44 have a lower estimated transmission line cost than Route 894, and 37 of those routes use neither Link F20 nor Link F23.

3. Airports and Airstrips

EXCEPTION 23: Finding of Fact 168 treats a favorable count as compliance with prudent avoidance.
Finding of Fact 166 correctly recites Rule 25.101(a)(6): prudent avoidance is "the limiting of exposures to electric and magnetic fields that can be avoided with reasonable investments of money and effort." Finding of Fact 168 then concludes that Route 894 "complies with the Commission's policy of prudent avoidance," resting on the count in Finding of Fact 167.
That misapplies the rule within the meaning of Rule 22.262(a)(1)(A), for three independent reasons.
First, no single routing factor is dispositive, and the courts have said so. The Office of Public Utility Counsel sets out the governing principle in this docket: the statutory factors "are stated in the broadest possible terms and are intended as legislative standards to guide the Commission in its administration of the certification process," some of the factors "may compete," and the Commission may be required to "adjust or accommodate the competing policies and interests involved." As Texland states, and as Hammack repeats, "[n]one of the statutory factors is intended to be absolute in the sense that any one shall prevail in all possible circumstances." The corollary is settled: the rule "grants the [Commission] the authority to consider and weigh a variety of factors ... in determining the most reasonable route," and a reviewing court will not substitute its judgment on which factor outweighs another. Neither proposition permits a single count to answer the question by itself.
Finding of Fact 168 makes one factor absolute. It moves from a count of habitable structures directly to a conclusion of compliance, with no intervening finding about what could reasonably have been avoided. That is the operation Texland and Hammack foreclose.
Second, the rule turns on avoidability, not on relative position in a count. Where filed alternatives in a different corridor avoid the exposure entirely at a cost difference of approximately 0.22% (see Exception 19), and where the count on which the comparison rests falls within its own margin of error, a favorable count does not establish that exposure was avoided.
Third, a count of structures is not a measure of exposure. The rule the ALJs quote in Finding of Fact 166 speaks of "the limiting of exposures to electric and magnetic fields." Finding of Fact 167 supplies a count of structures. The two are not the same quantity, and nothing in the findings bridges them.
A structure count records one binary fact: whether a structure stands inside 500 feet of a centerline. It does not record how many people occupy the structure, or for how many hours of the day or days of the year. Exposure, as the word is ordinarily used and as Rule 25.101(a)(6) uses it, depends on all of those.
The record establishes that the parties themselves understand this. Applicants' witness Marusak testified that "[a]ll things being equal ... if I can avoid a school, I'm certainly going to look to," PFD at 110. And the ALJs themselves wrote that "[r]outing options that will reasonably avoid population centers and other locations where people gather will also achieve this purpose." Neither statement is intelligible if a structure is a structure and a count of one is a count of one.
The routing methodology has no place to record the circumstance at all. Applicants' witness Marusak confirmed on cross-examination that the Environmental Assessment and routing study contain no reference to the April 12, 2022 EF-3 tornado that tracked through the Cedar Valley community along FM 2843; that the Governor declared Bell County a state disaster area the following day; and that approximately 70 homes and three church buildings were damaged. He confirmed that First Cedar Valley Baptist Church, which the community rebuilt after the tornado, sits approximately 700 feet from the proposed Link F20 centerline. He was then asked about the criteria themselves. Tr. Vol. 4 at 55:
Q. Your routing evaluation uses about 36 criteria. Among those criteria, is there any that would account for a corridor that has experienced a federally or state-declared natural disaster?
A. (Marusak) We don't have something specific to that. No, sir.
Q. Should we?
A. (Marusak) I'm not trying to be insensitive. But how long does that last? I mean, how long would that be good for? Is it ten years after? Twenty years after? Thirty years after? I think you do run into a certain problem to that extent.
Q. So is there any criteria that accounts for the recovery that's after?
A. (Marusak) No. We do not specifically have anything for that.
Mr. Howton does not suggest the witness was dismissive; the line-drawing difficulty he identifies is real, and he answered candidly. The significance is structural. A thirty-six-criterion evaluation that contains no variable for a declared disaster or for a community in active recovery will return the same score for the Cedar Valley corridor as for any other corridor with the same structure count. That is why the record on this point is silent, and it is why a favorable count cannot substitute for the avoidability inquiry the rule requires. Both witnesses were reasoning about who is inside and how many, which is to say, about exposure. The metric they then applied records none of it.
Applicants' own data confirms the aggregation. The table at PFD 144 disaggregates the Focus Route counts by structure type:

Every one of those categories contributes to the total on identical terms. Applicants' own Table 7-5 defines the "BGS" category as a "barn, garage, shed that may be occupied on a regular basis," a category admitted on a conditional. Mr. Howton asks the Commission to weight no category above another, and takes no position that any structure type deserves less protection than any other. Rule 25.101(a)(3) defines habitable structures to include churches, hospitals, nursing homes, and schools alongside dwellings, and draws no distinction among them. He asks only that the Commission not treat a number that measures none of these things as though it established compliance with a rule that speaks of exposure.
Third, the Proposal for Decision does not apply the count consistently. For Route 894 the count is the whole of the prudent-avoidance analysis: Finding of Fact 167 states the number and Finding of Fact 168 concludes compliance. The Commission has a working definition of community values, and it describes what the count omits. EXCEPTION 27: Finding of Fact 225 exempts the Project from the economic cost-benefit testing applicable to a project not established as necessary to meet reliability standards, on a premise Conclusion of Law 14 rejects.
Finding of Fact 225 states that "[t]he Project is a reliability project," and that as such the estimated cost to consumers and congestion-cost-savings analyses "are not required under Rule 25.101(b)(3)(A)(i) and (b)(3)(A)(ii)." Finding of Fact 227 confirms "the record contains no evidence quantifying either."
Finding of Fact 224 finds the opposite premise: "Applicants present the Project as one that will import power ... not that the proposed transmission facilities are necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards." Conclusion of Law 14 finds that the evidence does not establish necessity at all.
Those cannot both operate in Applicants' favor. If the Project is a reliability project, its necessity for reliability had to be proven and was not. If its necessity for reliability was not proven, PURA § 37.056(d) and Rule 25.101(b)(3)(A)(i) require an economic showing that Applicants concede they never made.
The record makes this documentary rather than inferential. The PBRP compares the three import path options twice: in the Executive Summary as Table E.1 (Bates 1884) and in the body as Table 7.6 (Bates 1939), the latter cited by the ALJs at PFD footnote 5. Both tables' first row records that the 345-kV, 500-kV, and 765-kV options each "Meets ERCOT and NERC Reliability Criteria: Yes," at total estimated 2038 costs of $12.95 billion, $15.32 billion, and $13.77 billion respectively.
Reliability therefore did not compel the 765-kV option. And the increment was selected on expressly economic grounds: Commission Staff recommended the 765-kV import paths because "[t]he long-term benefits associated with the 765 kV import paths justify the additional 22% estimated capital cost premium," describing the selection as a "forward-thinking policy decision." Project No. 55718, Item No. 106, at 7, adopted by Second Order Approving PBRP (Apr. 24, 2025).
Mr. Howton does not ask the Commission to order a different voltage. That is outside the scope of this Application. The point is narrower: the marginal investment the Commission approved was justified by a cost-benefit judgment made in a project docket outside any contested case, and Finding of Fact 225 now exempts that same investment from the economic cost-benefit requirements applicable to a project not established as necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards.
Requested relief. That Finding of Fact 225 be amended to state that any exemption from the economic tests is contingent on a demonstrated reliability necessity that Applicants failed to establish; and a conclusion of law that on this record the Commission cannot make the findings PURA § 37.056(d) requires.

EXCEPTION 29: The standard ordering paragraphs should require consultation and geoarchaeological assessment where the approved route crosses areas of high archeological potential.
Preliminary Order Issue 14 asks whether the best management practices standard in the Commission's electric CCN orders are adequate and, if not, what additional practices should be required. Applicants take the position that the standard language is adequate. The ALJs made one finding on the question, addressed to alternating-current interference.
The standard language already contemplates the work. Finding of Fact 244 provides that should a route be selected, Applicants will conduct a field assessment before beginning construction "to identify water resources, cultural resources, potential migratory bird issues, and threatened and endangered species' habitats disrupted by the transmission line," and will identify and comply with the necessary permits.
Two findings support making that assessment specific where the risk is highest. Finding of Fact 200 establishes that Route 894 crosses 54.34 miles of areas identified as having high potential for historical or archeological sites, 24.3% of its length. And the record establishes that formal designation is not the measure of significance: Applicants' witness "acknowledged that just because the area has not been formally identified as historically significant does not mean that it is insignificant or should be ignored." A cultural designation was assigned to one property during this proceeding, and another landowner testified that she was in the process of registering hers.
Where a route crosses a quarter of its length through modeled high-potential terrain, and where the record shows recorded designations emerging during the case rather than before it, a general instruction to identify cultural resources may not produce the survey the circumstance calls for. Deeply buried deposits are not identifiable from the surface, and disturbance is not reversible.
The record shows the gap concretely on a link of the recommended route. Applicants' witness Marusak confirmed that the cultural resources review for Link F20 was a desktop review of the Texas Historical Commission's recorded-site database; that Table 7-3 reports Link F20 crossing approximately 3,831 feet of high archaeological or historical site potential while reporting zero recorded cultural resource sites; and that no field archaeological survey of the F20 corridor was conducted before the route was selected. Asked whether the high-potential designation exists precisely because corridors of that kind contain deeply buried archaeological deposits that a desktop database review cannot detect, he agreed. Link F20 lies within the study area of the Buttermilk Creek complex; Mr. Marusak testified that while he was "not aware of the specifics," he was "aware of a lot of archeological sites in this part of the study area."
Mr. Howton does not ask the Commission to find that any particular site exists. The request is prospective and applies to whichever route is approved.
Requested relief. That the standard ordering paragraphs be supplemented to provide that, where the approved route crosses areas the Environmental Assessment identifies as having high potential for historical or archeological sites, Applicants shall consult the Texas Historical Commission and complete a geoarchaeological assessment of those segments before ground disturbance, and shall comply with any resulting survey, avoidance, or mitigation requirements.

EXCEPTION 31: If the Commission approves the Application, it should adopt here the landowner-consent deviation paragraph it adopted on August 28, 2026.
This exception is conditional. It applies only if the Commission declines the ALJs' denial recommendation. Mr. Howton's primary position remains denial, and nothing in this exception should be read as consent to approval.
On August 27, 2026, Chairman Gleeson recommended in both Docket No. 59029 and Docket No. 59315 that the Commission delete its standard ordering paragraph barring more-than-minor route deviations and replace it with a paragraph permitting them on two conditions. His stated reason was that "the integrity of these types of properties should be preserved and property boundaries respected whenever possible," that "Oncor should avoid bisecting properties when reasonable accommodations can be made," and that the utility "should be allowed to work with affected landowners on the ground to accommodate route deviations requested by landowners." The substituted paragraph reads:
"Oncor must be permitted to deviate from the approved route in any instance in which the deviation would be more than a minor deviation, but only if the following two conditions are met. First, Oncor must receive consent from all landowners who would be affected by the deviation, regardless of whether the affected landowner received notice of or participated in this proceeding. Second, the deviation must result in a reasonably direct path towards the terminus of the line and not cause an unreasonable increase in cost or delay the project. Unless these two conditions are met, this paragraph does not authorize Oncor to deviate from the approved route except as allowed by the other ordering paragraphs in this Order."
Two features of that paragraph make it particularly apt in this docket, and Mr. Howton adopts it rather than proposing his own.
First, it addresses the notice failure the ALJs found, at the only stage where a remedy is still available. The condition that consent be obtained from all affected landowners "regardless of whether the affected landowner received notice of or participated in this proceeding" is directed precisely at the class the ALJs identified: owners who were brought into the project by post-meeting link additions and who had no meeting at which to identify constraints. The Commission has already determined, one week before this filing, that such landowners should have a voice at the deviation stage even though they had none earlier. If the Commission approves this Application without curing the notice defect, that paragraph is the minimum accommodation consistent with its own August 28 reasoning.
Second, it is the mechanism by which the Route 296 defect is cured. Exception 15 shows that Route 296's single identified disqualifying feature, the centerline running within 500 feet of Florence Elementary School and two churches on Link F34, is curable by a northward adjustment within already-noticed Tract 2361. The Chairman's paragraph supplies the procedural vehicle for exactly that kind of adjustment, on landowner consent, without a further CCN amendment. The ALJs treated the Route 296 defect as fixed and disqualifying. It is neither.
A second, smaller accommodation the Commission has ordered before. If the Commission approves a route using Link F20, Mr. Howton asks that it require optimum phasing of the conductors along that link. Optimum phasing reduces magnetic-field strength at the edge of the right-of-way through conductor arrangement alone, at no change in alignment and no additional right-of-way. The Commission has ordered it in prior certificate proceedings. Application of Cross Texas Transmission, LLC to Amend its Certificate of Convenience and Necessity for the Limestone to Gibbons Creek 345-kV Transmission Line, Docket No. 44649, Finding of Fact 237 (Jan. 13, 2016); see OPUC Post-Hearing Initial Br. at 6 (Item No. 6179). It is directly responsive to the rule the Commission applies at Findings of Fact 166 through 168: prudent avoidance is "the limiting of exposures ... that can be avoided with reasonable investments of money and effort," 16 TAC § 25.101(a)(6), and phasing is the least costly such investment available on an approved alignment. Mr. Howton does not present it as a substitute for route selection. He presents it as the mitigation that remains if route selection goes against him.
Requested relief. If the Commission approves the Application, that it (i) adopt in this docket the ordering paragraph quoted above, in place of the standard ordering paragraph prohibiting more-than-minor deviations, and (ii) state in the accompanying discussion that the paragraph is available to accommodate the school and church proximities on Link F34 identified at PFD 147. First, on the scope of HB 5066. Second, on the fiscal record. The Attorney General notes that the Legislative Budget Board's fiscal note for HB 5066 "included no additional anticipated costs to the state or consumers in its five-year forecast," and contrasts S.B. 2012 from the same session, whose fiscal note did state that build-out costs "would be recovered in the utility rates." That bears on Exception 27 and on Section IX.A generally: if the Legislature was not told the plan would cost what it costs, the Commission's obligation to test cost to consumers under its own rule is heightened, not relieved.

That is the office and the division through which the State appears in administrative-law litigation.        The seven-day requirement for ERCOT directive materials is not a matter of internal

preference: PURA § 39.1514(b)(3) directs that the Commission "by rule shall ... establish a

reasonable timeline for the release before a commission meeting of discussion materials relevant

to any proposed commission directives included as agenda items for that meeting." The

Legislature required advance release of discussion materials for directives to ERCOT. No

comparable requirement governs the document that decides whether a landowner's property is

crossed.
       The asymmetry is sharpest against Rule 22.262(d)(3). A party must request oral

argument seven days before the open meeting. A memorandum proposing to delete that party's

supporting findings may issue seventeen hours before it. A party who did not anticipate the

memorandum a week in advance has, by operation of the Commission's own timing rules, no

mechanism to be heard on it at all.
